free-compute-dev\\n\\nAn autonomous software-development harness built on the firm's stated economics:\\n\\n- **Default effort = contributed compute.** Patch generation and iteration run on\\n  the cheapest sufficient endpoint currently admitted by LISS (today Groq, Gemini,\\n  GitHub Models, OpenRouter when available, and later private GPU workers).\\n- **`claude -p` is the gated exception**, not the default — used as a quality gate and\\n  for problems above a difficulty threshold, because it is the expensive resource.\\n\\nThis is a persistent software-production fabric, not a conversational coding\\nwrapper. A caller can submit an objective and leave. The fabric observes the\\nterritory, contracts parallel inference, executes bounded tools, verifies\\ncandidates, integrates one without overwriting concurrent work, and records the\\nsuccessful trajectory for reuse.\\n\\n## Live result\\n\\nOn 2026-07-19, three isolated workers contracted Groq, Gemini, and GitHub Models\\nthrough the persistent LISS broker. Gemini independently navigated to `src/executor.mjs`, derived a two-edit\\nrepair for a real temporary-directory leak, passed the package suite in\\nisolation, and the runtime atomically integrated and reverified it. The\\nbounded residue was resubmitted through the queue to Claude with provider-enforced\\nJSON Schema. Claude inspected the test and runtime, authored the regression, and\\nthe queue integrated it after verification. The resulting 26-test suite proves\\nearly quorum, dead-worker claim abandonment, protected-border integration, and the\\ndurable carrier itself. The failed cheap trajectory remains evidence for future\\ntask-class pricing instead of being hidden.\\n\\n## Operating surfaces\\n\\n- `run-union-dev-mission mission.json` runs one objective through parallel isolated\\n  tool workers and a verification/integration gate.\\n- `run-union-dev-program program.json` asks multiple cloud planners for acyclic\\n  mission DAGs, validates them, and executes the cheapest valid plan until the\\n  declared program acceptance command passes.\\n- `submit-union-dev-mission mission.json` and `run-union-dev-worker` provide a\\n  durable queue, claims, heartbeats, stale-claim recovery, and unattended service.\\n- `abandon-union-dev-mission exact-id reason` terminally settles work whose worker\\n  was deliberately stopped, preventing stale recovery from purchasing obsolete\\n  inference again.\\n- LISS's persistent broker accepts batches through a filesystem spool as well as a\\n  Unix socket. Sandboxed workers need neither network access nor provider keys;\\n  they atomically signal jobs through the spool while the one broker owns cloud\\n  access, pricing, concurrency, replay, and the append-only settlement journal.\\n\\nEach worker can `list_files`, `search`, `read`, apply exact edits, run the declared\\nverification/acceptance gates, and invoke only commands pre-admitted by the mission.\\nCandidate workspaces are copies; integration compares source digests and classifies\\na concurrent source change as a protected border instead of overwriting it.\\n\\nAn unresolved base phase is automatically re-contracted as `software-engineering`\\nwork requiring schema-validated actions. Unless a\\nmission explicitly declines semantic review, three independently sharded cloud\\nreviewers compare the changed source to the original objective and constraints.\\nA valid-review majority is required. Facts: one process must own the sole shared scheduler and append-only journal; jobs are JSON objects with globally unique IDs; results settle asynchronously; durable completed IDs replay without provider spend; queue/seen sets are bounded; EOF/SIGTERM currently drains; malformed lines are contained; one process lock excludes another journal owner. Multiple autonomous colony clients must connect without launching the broker. The socket must remain host-local, preserve per-client result isolation, survive client disconnect after admission, prevent an untrusted client from shutting down the broker, and bound line bytes/connections/write buffers. "content": "LISS has a legacy ActivityStreams service contract that synchronously spawns child provider CLIs, and a newer persistent cheapest-sufficient broker over a local Unix socket. The broker returns immediate admission receipts, settles asynchronously, journals results, replays by job ID plus payload digest, and bounds queue/concurrency/RPM/attempts. Root law permits LISS to own its service-specific ActivityStreams semantic contract but reserves reusable network ActivityPub transport to a separately hireable provider. A separate metered-inference-tollbooth owns x402 authorization verification and truthfully does not claim on-chain broadcast. Proposed smallest repair: run a service-specific ActivityStreams adapter inside the one persistent LISS broker process. It handles addressed Offer<ServiceSolicitation>, provider-authored digest-bound Offer<ExecutableServiceOffer>, Accept<ServiceContract> with actor-bound attenuated capability, and actor-bound Question<InferenceResultQuery>. Acceptance maps to broker.admit and returns immediately as Accept<InferenceSubmissionResult>; inquiry later returns the terminal record or typed not-settled refusal. Provider offers, contracts, submission responses, and ownership bindings are append-only LISS records and replay safely across restart. Raw NDJSON stays classified A2A; ActivityStreams envelopes are the semantic inter-enterprise face over the local carrier. Network federation is deferred to the missing ActivityPub provider. x402 stays outside LISS. Identify critical changes or reject this design. Never recommend another scheduler or synchronous waiting."

This theorem is the structural ground for inter-session-messaging's causal discipline. It is the substrate-internal counterpart to [per-stream-chunk-delivery-is-fifo-projection-of-event-log](per-stream-chunk-delivery-is-fifo-projection-of-event-log.md), which establishes per-channel FIFO for stdout/stderr chunks streamed over WebSocket. The two theorems share the per-channel-only ordering shape; they differ in mechanism and grain. The chunk-delivery theorem invokes RFC 6455 transport FIFO to pin a wall-clock delivery sequence at the subscriber. This theorem makes a weaker but cleaner claim: it pins a structural total order on per-channel messages via `authored-at-ord` and leaves wall-clock surfacing-sequence to the consumer's processing discipline. The reason for the weaker form is that inter-session messaging's surfacing path is internal to the substrate's rule machinery — it is not a single ordered transport — so the substrate-level guarantee that survives all internal scheduling choices is the order on the cell-data, not the order of rule firings.

**Claim.** Fix a `(session-id, process-handle, stream)` triple $T$. Let $\Sigma_n$ denote the substrate's event log up to ord $n$, and let $\mathrm{chunks}_T(\Sigma_n)$ denote the subsequence of $\Sigma_n$ consisting of `stream-chunk` events whose `(session-id, process-handle, stream)` equals $T$, in event-ord order. Fix a subscriber $A$ holding a single WebSocket subscription with filter selecting triple $T$, observed across an interval $[\mathrm{ord}_a, \mathrm{ord}_b]$ during which the connection is continuously open and the substrate's emit path for $T$ is operating normally. Let $V \subseteq \mathrm{chunks}_T(\Sigma_n) \cap [\mathrm{ord}_a, \mathrm{ord}_b]$ denote the chunks $A$ is authorized to see — those whose authorization premise $A$'s capability fiber satisfies (per [modal-restriction-as-substrate-authorization-primitive](modal-restriction-as-substrate-authorization-primitive.md)) and whose contents are not encryption-region-restricted out of $A$'s vantage (per [encryption-as-visibility-restriction-via-invisible-automorphism](encryption-as-visibility-restriction-via-invisible-automorphism.md)).

3. *Within the connection's lifetime*, a chunk $c \in \mathrm{chunks}_T(\Sigma_n) \cap [\mathrm{ord}_a, \mathrm{ord}_b]$ omitted from $V$ is detectable by $A$ as a gap in the observed `chunk-seq` sequence **whenever there exists a later chunk in $V$ with strictly greater `chunk-seq`** (the omission is then bracketed and visible as a missing integer between two observed values). Detected gaps within a healthy single-connection interval are attributable to either authorization restriction or encryption-region restriction (these being the only two omission mechanisms admissible inside such an interval). Terminal-suffix omissions — a contiguous tail of $\mathrm{chunks}_T$ omitted with no later observed chunk — are not detectable from the chunk-seq sequence alone; the subscriber needs the §3 `stream-end` sentinel or an out-of-band signal to distinguish "stream ended" from "tail omitted." Gaps caused by transport interruption, subscription error, or connection close fall outside the claim's scope and require the subscriber to distinguish them via the WebSocket close-code (§5 of the WebSocket spec).

**Part 2: subscriber delivery preserves event-ord.** The dev spec ([`process/session-output-streaming.md`](../../../../../../../../../operations/engineering/tools/predication-computer/pypredcomp/docs/dev/specs/process/session-output-streaming.md) §4 + [`network/websocket.md`](../../../../../../../../../operations/engineering/tools/predication-computer/pypredcomp/docs/dev/specs/network/websocket.md) §2) specifies that subscriber delivery on the `substrate-events.v1` subprotocol emits one event per WebSocket frame, and that the substrate's emit path drives frames out in event-log scan order.

The capability filter applied per [modal-restriction-as-substrate-authorization-primitive](modal-restriction-as-substrate-authorization-primitive.md) (the WebSocket §4 capability gate) is likewise an elementwise positive predicate: it admits a chunk to $A$'s view iff $A$'s capability fiber satisfies the chunk's authorization premise, with no dependence on prior or subsequent chunks. Composition of elementwise filters is again an elementwise filter, preserving order.

WebSocket per RFC 6455 (cited by [`network/websocket.md`](../../../../../../../../../operations/engineering/tools/predication-computer/pypredcomp/docs/dev/specs/network/websocket.md) §1) delivers frames within a single open connection in the order the sender wrote them. Within the connection's lifetime $[\mathrm{ord}_a, \mathrm{ord}_b]$, therefore, $A$ observes $V$ in event-ord order, which by Part 1 equals `chunk-seq` order.

- **One subscription = one WebSocket connection.** The FIFO guarantee is per-connection. A subscriber that reconnects mid-stream sees the chunks delivered after reconnect; chunks delivered to the prior connection are not redelivered. The chunk-seq gap then signals the connection-boundary loss, not an authorization restriction. (Implementations that wish to backfill from event-log replay are exercising [streaming-replay-equivalence](streaming-replay-equivalence.md), which is a separate guarantee.)

**Part 4: Transport switching mid-federation.** When a federation switches transports (e.g., a TCP connection drops and reconnects via WebSocket), in-flight messages from the dropped connection are retransmitted on the new connection. Per [federation-convergence](federation-convergence.md)'s order-independence, retransmissions are safe — duplicates are deduplicated by hash, missed-original-deliveries are recovered by the retransmission. The converged state is unaffected.

- **Transport upgrades without downtime.** Switching from one transport to another (HTTP → WebSocket for lower latency, TCP → TLS-TCP for added security) does not require federation-state migration. The substrate continues federation seamlessly across the transport change.

Joan Acker's "Hierarchies, Jobs, Bodies: A Theory of Gendered Organizations" (1990) inaugurates feminist organizational theory. Organizational structures are not gender-neutral containers; they are built on an image of "the worker" that is implicitly male — a being with no body, no sexuality, no obligations to reproduction or care, available for unlimited hours, with a wife at home managing his biological needs. The organizational structure (schedules, career paths, advancement criteria) is designed for this body and this life. Acker identifies five processes that reproduce gender in organizations: (1) the division of labor (gender-segregated occupations); (2) cultural symbols and images (masculine metaphors of warfare, conquest, competition); (3) workplace interactions (men interrupting, taking space; women's emotional labor and deferential listening); (4) individual identities (people internalize gendered identities through organizational life); (5) organizational logic (the separation of public paid work from private home, the definition of commitment as unlimited availability).

For more sophisticated NPC behavior, Discworld implements an event system: NPCs can subscribe to event classes (`event_listen_say()`, `event_person_tell()`). When a say happens in a room, the NPC's event handler is called with the speaker and text. The NPC can then decide whether to respond, start combat, or ignore the message.

This implements **M4** (every message names its receivers) with asymmetry: a player's say is broadcast to all objects in the room, but which objects *care* is determined by their subscriptions. NPCs are not forced to hear everything — they can filter by listener pattern (e.g., a shopkeeper hears only customers, a guard hears only unauthorized intruders).

MUD emits events for every table write operation. Off-chain indexers listen to these events and maintain SQL databases that mirror the on-chain state.
1. Listening to all Store_SetRecord, Store_SpliceStaticData, etc. events

Events include the table ID, the key, and the new value. Client indexers listen to these events, replicate the Store into a relational database, and serve queries to game clients. The client never needs to decode Solidity ABI or deal with smart contract state variables — it queries a normal database that is synchronized with on-chain state via event replay.

When a system writes to the Store, an event is emitted. The indexer listens to these events, parses them, and writes the changes to a relational database (PostgreSQL, for example). The client's TypeScript code queries this database via an API, not the blockchain.

When a player wants to take an action — move, attack, cast a spell — the client sends a transaction to call the appropriate System. The transaction is signed, sent to the blockchain, mined, and emitted as events. The indexer picks up those events and updates the database. The client's state listener sees the database changed and updates the UI.
No data migration needed. No careful coordination of state schema changes. Logic is ephemeral; data is persistent.

The totality of this subjugation is conveyed in the crushing testimonies of those who experienced it: Auschwitz survivor Elie Wiesel listened to his own father cry out for him while being beaten to death, yet was unable to muster a response.34 Filip Müller painfully watched as 4,000 Auschwitz inmates knowingly walked into the gas chambers despite the prolonged efforts of some to agitate them into resistance.35 Tadeusz Borowski recalls working alongside 10,000 workers when a truck full of naked women slowly rolled by calling out for help: “‘Save us! Save us!’… Not one of us made a move, not one of us lifted a hand.”36 These testimonies are powerful gestures towards the depravity of the “concentration universe” and the extent to which it violently precluded the potential for defiance. These are not stories of individual passivity — they are stories of systematic disempowerment.

Perhaps more than anything else, the physical conditions of the Lagers played a role in the suppression of defiance. An explication of this sort could be long and brutal, but suffice it to say that being kept forever on the brink of starvation, worked beyond the capacities of the human body, exposed daily to wanton acts of cruelty, subjected to year-round elemental onslaught, and being perpetually enveloped in pestilence and disease, has the capacity to turn human bodies into emaciated shells devoid of will power or physical strength. Then I'll probably dive straight into trying to set up a socket server and the other parts of a basic MUD engine. (I'll explain those when I get to them.)

Services might otherwise be called daemons. They're mini-programs that provide the capabilities that make the engine go. For example, in the Python version of qtMUD, there is a MUDSocket service, which controls the socket server which clients use to send requests via telnet, and the Talker service. (The Talker service doesn't actually need to be a service, so we'll ignore it for now.)
After being loaded, qtMUD starts itself, which means starting each of its now-loaded services. In the case of the MUDSocket service, this means binding itself to the appropriate port.

Every tick(), each scheduled event is processed, meaning the relevant subscription is called with the matching arguments. Also, every active service that has a `tick()` function has its `tick()` called. For MUDSocket, that means reading any requests that have come in, and sending out any responses that have been queued.

On the next tick, the MUDSocket service starts its tick by looking at every active connection it has. It would notice that one is new, and it would accept the connection, which would be a socket object and the network addres the object is at. It'd create a new client Thing and give it:
-   an `addr` quality set to the socket's network address
While the person was typing, qtMUD kept calling its `tick()`, which kept calling the MUDSocket service's `tick()`, but there wasn't anything to do so nothign happened.

But after hitting enter, the MUDSocket would catch that there was new data on that connection on its next `tick()`, and convert it to a string. It'd look up the client Thing associated with that connection, and set it as the value for that Thing's `recv_buffer` quality.
The second step is fleshing out a MUDSocket service: something that can start, run, tick, and shutdown, just like the engine. It doesn't have to do anything more for now.

Services might otherwise be called daemons. They're mini-programs that provide the capabilities that make the engine go. For example, in the Python version of qtMUD, there is a MUDSocket service, which controls the socket server which clients use to send requests via telnet, and the Talker service. (The Talker service doesn't actually need to be a service, so we'll ignore it for now.)
After being loaded, qtMUD starts itself, which means starting each of its now-loaded services. In the case of the MUDSocket service, this means binding itself to the appropriate port.

Every tick(), each scheduled event is processed, meaning the relevant subscription is called with the matching arguments. Also, every active service that has a `tick()` function has its `tick()` called. For MUDSocket, that means reading any requests that have come in, and sending out any responses that have been queued.

On the next tick, the MUDSocket service starts its tick by looking at every active connection it has. It would notice that one is new, and it would accept the connection, which would be a socket object and the network addres the object is at. It'd create a new client Thing and give it:
-   an `addr` quality set to the socket's network address
While the person was typing, qtMUD kept calling its `tick()`, which kept calling the MUDSocket service's `tick()`, but there wasn't anything to do so nothign happened.

But after hitting enter, the MUDSocket would catch that there was new data on that connection on its next `tick()`, and convert it to a string. It'd look up the client Thing associated with that connection, and set it as the value for that Thing's `recv_buffer` quality.
The second step is fleshing out a MUDSocket service: something that can start, run, tick, and shutdown, just like the engine. It doesn't have to do anything more for now.
Tie in starting, running, and stopping the MUDSocket service with the main engine.

<p>PRAXONIC WORLDBUILDING GUIDE <em>A Recursive Framework for Making Meaningful Worlds from Pressure</em> &mdash; ## I. INTRODUCTION <em>You are not creating a place. You are tracing a deformation.</em> This guide teaches a method of world creation that begins not with lore, genre, or aesthetics, but with <strong>pressure</strong>. In this framework, a <strong>world</strong> is not a map, a backstory, or a set of cultures. It is a <strong>field</strong>—a living surface shaped by tension, memory, and contradiction. It behaves. It resists. It shifts when touched. The method here is called <strong>praxonic worldmaking</strong>, and it grows from a system called <strong>praxonic interpretation</strong>: a minimal logic for how things emerge, change, and fold under recursive pressure. You do not &ldquo;invent&rdquo; a world. You <strong>interpret</strong> a pressure until a field appears. You follow that field until it begins to emit trace. You record those traces until they produce <strong>actors, zones, misalignments, ghosts, care structures, silence events</strong>, and other system behaviors. That is your world. It does not need to explain itself. It only needs to <strong>persist under contradiction</strong>. &mdash; ### Who is this for? - Writers building narrative systems grounded in logistical or ethical realism - TTRPG designers and GMs who want tension-first, world-as-character mechanics - Memory workers designing shared testimony environments - LARPers, performance artists, collective documentarians - Fictional worldbuilders who want to say less and evoke more - You &mdash; ### What kinds of worlds can this method produce? - A refugee clinic with a broken radio, and too much gauze - A decaying lighthouse no one wants to admit is a god - A corporate loyalty program that becomes the only way to survive winter - A haunted apartment building where the ghosts are eviction notices - A 15-year stretch of drought told as a memory game - A cave system where every echo was someone’s confession - Your neighborhood - Your inbox - Your dream from last week Praxonic worldmaking is not bound to realism, fantasy, or speculative fiction. It works anywhere pressure exists, which means <strong>everywhere</strong>. &mdash; ### What does this guide do? It gives you tools to: - Recognize the core praxon at the heart of your world - Model how that praxon becomes emissions, then trace - Define zones by how pressure behaves there - Shape characters as local alignment systems - Track contradiction as signal, not error - Use decay, silence, refusal, and care as building blocks - Build stories, sessions, loops, or memory events as <strong>recursive outcomes</strong>, not linear sequences This guide does not give you templates. It gives you tension structures. &mdash; ### What will I end up with? A world that behaves like a living pressure field. One where everything means something—but not all at once. A world that can contain friction, memory, noise, decay, contradiction, care, and humor. A world that gets more usable the more broken it becomes. &mdash; ### How do I use this guide? You can read it linearly, use it modularly, or treat it like a signal you only half-hear until it resonates with a project you already started and forgot. You do not have to believe in it. You only have to trace where it leads. The next section defines the core system: <strong>Praxonic Interpretation</strong>. &mdash; ## II. CORE GRAMMAR: PRAXONIC INTERPRETATION <em>“Every act is a response to something already under pressure.”</em> Praxonic interpretation is the minimal system by which a world can be <strong>read, constructed, and recursively unfolded</strong> from pressure. At its core, this system defines: - What kinds of <strong>entities</strong> exist in a recursive world - What <strong>relations</strong> occur between them - How <strong>change</strong>, <strong>meaning</strong>, and <strong>instability</strong> emerge as system behavior It is <strong>not</strong> a symbolic language. It is a structural logic for making any world—real or imagined—behave like something under tension. &mdash; ### 1. CORE ENTITY: THE PRAXON A <strong>praxon</strong> is a unit of unresolved pressure. It is the smallest readable element of a world-under-formation. It is <strong>not content</strong>. It is <strong>pre-semantic</strong>: behavior before definition. Praxons do not &ldquo;mean.&rdquo; They emit. They deform. They recur. A praxon may be: - A border crossing no one agrees exists - A prayer repeated so often it becomes scheduling - A broken faucet that changes how a house speaks - The moment someone realizes the radio isn’t broken—it’s unplugged Worlds begin with praxons. They do not describe conditions. They <strong>are</strong> conditions. &mdash; ### 2. SYSTEM LOOP: PRAXONIC FIELD DYNAMICS The world is built from this recursive cycle: Praxon → Emission → Trace → Field → Alignment → Path → Emission Or more mechanically: 1. <strong>A praxon emits</strong> a deformation (an act, error, signal, silence) 2. That emission leaves <strong>trace</strong>—a distortion of the surrounding world 3. All trace combines into a <strong>field</strong>—the condition of the world at any moment 4. <strong>Actors</strong> become legible via their alignment to the local field 5. Alignment + field = possible <strong>path</strong> (response/behavior) 6. That path produces new emission 7. The loop continues, recursively Each iteration either increases coherence or generates <strong>irresolved noise</strong> (IRN)—which accumulates into pressure again. &mdash; ### 3. KEY COMPONENTS Each part of the loop is a functional entity. #### ➤ Emission Any output from a praxon or aligned actor. May be action, refusal, signal, breakdown, memory. #### ➤ Trace The residual deformation left in the field by an emission. Trace decays unless retained or reinforced. Decay is not disappearance—it is transformation. #### ➤ Field The sum of all potential trace. A dynamic, living pressure environment. Contains alignment conditions, actor legibility, volatility zones. #### ➤ Alignment A local actor’s modulation to the field. Alignment determines which paths are visible, plausible, survivable. #### ➤ Path A behavior that can emerge from the intersection of field and alignment. Not chosen freely—conditioned by pressure. All acts are pathings. Even silence. #### ➤ Irresolved Noise (IRN) When emissions cannot be aligned, retained, or decayed. IRN remains in the field as recursive contradiction. It generates distortion, myth, violence, ghost-behavior, confusion, and memory split. &mdash; ### 4. RELATIONAL PROPERTIES - <strong>Field defines potential.</strong> The world doesn’t contain meaning—it <strong>pressurizes</strong> it. - <strong>Actors do not pre-exist the field.</strong> They emerge via pressure readability. - <strong>Paths are conditioned.</strong> Choice is not freedom. It is coherence under constraint. - <strong>Resolution is local.</strong> An emission that is signal in one alignment may be noise in another. - <strong>Decay is not loss.</strong> Decay produces change in form, not always disappearance. - <strong>Contradiction is content.</strong> Do not smooth it. Fold it. &mdash; ### 5. PRACTICAL USE When building or interpreting a world: 1. Identify praxons 2. Determine emissions (what’s happening under pressure) 3. Track trace and decay (what remains, what changes) 4. Map the field (what behaviors the world permits) 5. Construct or observe alignments (who can act how) 6. Read or trigger paths (what happens next) 7. Accept IRN (where pressure will not resolve cleanly) This is how a fantasy village, a cyberpunk megacity, or your friend’s kitchen becomes a praxonic world. &mdash; In the next section, we’ll use this grammar to <strong>form worlds</strong> from praxons. This is the start of <strong>Praxonic Worldmaking</strong>. &mdash; ## III. WORLD FORMATION: FROM PRAXON TO FIELD <em>“You’re not inventing a world. You’re tracking where something gave.”</em> Worlds built through praxonic interpretation emerge from pressure, not premise. They do not begin as genre, theme, or story—they begin as <strong>rupture</strong>, <strong>weight</strong>, or <strong>distortion</strong>. You are not placing pieces. You are recognizing faultlines and following them as they fold. This section provides a <strong>method</strong> for constructing a usable, recursive world from a single or nested praxon. &mdash; ### STEP 1: SELECT A PRAXON Start with a pressure—an unresolved contradiction, demand, or misalignment. A praxon is <strong>not a theme</strong>. It is a <strong>condition under tension</strong>, readable through action or refusal. Examples: - “The clinic keeps running even though the signal stopped weeks ago.” - “The castle’s water source is poisoned, but no one can admit it.” - “Everyone agrees the event happened. No one agrees on when.” - “The mountain is sacred, but it’s moved five times this year.” - “This family does not talk about the fourth child.” ⚠️ Avoid defining too much too early. Let the praxon shape what comes next. &mdash; ### STEP 2: GENERATE INITIAL EMISSIONS Ask: <strong>What actions, refusals, silences, or contradictions emerge under this pressure?</strong> Emissions may be: - Physical: a door sealed, a pot boiling, a child hiding - Social: an apology not offered, a rule misapplied - Informational: a rumor, a transmission, a misreading - Recursive: a repetition that doesn’t resolve Document at least 3 emissions. You can use text, sketch, scene fragment, mechanical rule, etc. &mdash; ### STEP 3: TRACE &amp; DECAY Each emission leaves <strong>trace</strong>—residual change. Trace deforms the world. Decay governs its persistence. For each emission: - What change does it leave behind? - What happens as that change decays? - What happens if it doesn&rsquo;t? Mark trace density: - <strong>High trace</strong> = memory-laden, emotionally volatile, visibly deformed - <strong>Low trace</strong> = ephemeral, ghosting, easily forgotten but deeply recursive Decay types: - Fast (e.g., hunger, blood trail, mood swing) - Medium (e.g., emotional rupture, supply loss, spoken insult) - Slow (e.g., ideology, superstition, long-term disrepair) &mdash; ### STEP 4: SHAPE THE FIELD Now aggregate all trace into a <strong>field</strong>: the pressure environment your world inhabits. Fields include: - <strong>Zones of volatility</strong> (conflict, error, risk) - <strong>Stabilizers</strong> (rituals, infrastructure, relationships) - <strong>Retention points</strong> (places, people, routines that resist decay) - <strong>IRN sinks</strong> (locations or memories where resolution fails repeatedly) The field is <strong>not geography</strong>. It is an environment of deformation. 📍 You can map it as a region, a building, a political system, or an emotion. The important part is how it <strong>behaves</strong>, not what it looks like. &mdash; ### STEP 5: LOCAL ALIGNMENTS Actors do not pre-exist the field—they emerge through readable alignment. For each part of the field: - Who (or what) becomes legible under that pressure? - What alignments become visible, plausible, unstable? - What actions are permitted or impossible from those alignments? You’re not defining characters yet. You’re modeling <strong>what types of action the world allows</strong>, and who survives that logic. Examples: - “Anyone who speaks the old dialect is assumed to be smuggling intel.” - “Repairing the radio means inheriting all the rumors it has failed to carry.” - “The priest can’t walk in the shrine anymore, but the children still play there.” &mdash; ### STEP 6: DEFINE PATH STRUCTURES A <strong>path</strong> is what becomes possible to do under the pressure of a field. Paths emerge from: - Alignment × Field Condition - Friction between trace and decay - Recursive IRN buildup - Silent thresholds (what is <em>almost</em> said) You’re designing <strong>behavior vectors</strong>, not scripted scenes. Types of path: - Recursion path: someone repeats what didn’t work - Refusal path: someone denies the field&rsquo;s logic - Drift path: someone alters alignment through pressure - Break path: contradiction accumulates until something tears Paths should not be predictable. They should be inevitable. &mdash; ### STEP 7: NAME THE WORLD Only now should you name the world, and even then, maybe not. If you must: - Use what the actors would call it - Use a nickname, frequency, smell, or gesture - Use a contradiction that can’t be resolved The name is not ownership. It is <strong>trace</strong>. &mdash; At this point, you have a full system: - A praxon - A series of emissions - A trace field with decay and retention - A behavioral logic for actors - Recursion patterns and IRN hotspots - A field responsive to care, refusal, and fracture This is your world. It is ready to emit. &mdash; ## IV. ACTORS &amp; AGENCIES <em>“They’re not protagonists. They’re readable distortions in the field.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, an <strong>actor</strong> is not someone with backstory, motivation, or moral arc. An actor is a <strong>form under pressure</strong>—a repeatable behavior pattern made visible by the field. They may be human, animal, machine, weather system, memory fragment, or rumor. What matters is their <strong>alignment</strong> and how they <strong>emit</strong> under tension. This section offers a toolkit for building, interpreting, and deploying actors within a praxonic world. &mdash; ### 1. ACTOR DEFINITION <strong>Actor</strong> = <em>Readable response system under local field conditions</em> Actors: - Do not pre-exist the field - Are defined by their alignment (how they “fit” the current pressure) - Emerge through trace saturation, ritual repetition, or behavioral recursion - May change alignment—becoming unstable, contradictory, or IRN-generating - May vanish when pressure resolves or shifts elsewhere An actor <strong>is not</strong> a symbol. It is a <strong>function</strong>. &mdash; ### 2. FUNCTION TYPES Actors express function through their <strong>role in the pressure loop</strong>. Common actor functions: - <strong>Stabilizer</strong> — absorbs pressure through repetition (e.g., the janitor who boils gauze) - <strong>Emitter</strong> — creates new emissions, intentionally or not (e.g., a child who won’t stop broadcasting) - <strong>Retention Node</strong> — holds trace against decay (e.g., a box of letters no one opens) - <strong>Distorter</strong> — reshapes field readings, creates misalignment (e.g., a leader who speaks five truths at once) - <strong>Echo / Ghost</strong> — reactivates decayed trace unpredictably (e.g., a frequency that replays arguments from last winter) You may assign multiple functions to a single actor. Function determines how the actor <strong>influences and is influenced by</strong> the field. &mdash; ### 3. ALIGNMENT BEHAVIOR Each actor is constantly shifting alignment with the field. <strong>Alignment determines:</strong> - What paths the actor can take - What actions they can perceive as viable - How others interpret their emissions - Whether their presence increases or relieves IRN Alignment may be: - <strong>In-phase</strong> — actor behaves legibly under current field pressure - <strong>Out-of-phase</strong> — actor emits noise, contradiction, or recursive error - <strong>Over-aligned</strong> — actor behaves so perfectly they become brittle, unstable - <strong>Under-aligned</strong> — actor cannot be read, evoking silence, refusal, or myth Alignment is not moral. It’s thermodynamic. &mdash; ### 4. DESIGN PROMPT TABLES Use these prompts to generate or reconfigure actors in any world: #### Emergence - What pressure created this actor? - Were they always here, or did something call them into shape? - What trace are they carrying? #### Modulation - How do they handle decay? - What retention behaviors do they perform, intentionally or not? - What parts of the field do they distort just by existing? #### Behavior - What emission patterns repeat around them? - Who tries to align with them—and fails? - What do they silence by showing up? #### Disappearance - What would make them unreadable again? - What fold are they holding closed? - If they left, what wouldn’t decay? &mdash; ### 5. SAMPLE ACTOR FORM Use this schema to create characters that function as systems, not tropes. [Name or Type] - Function: (Stabilizer, Emitter, etc.) - Alignment State: (In-phase / Out-of-phase / Over-aligned / Under-aligned) - Emission Pattern: [list recurring actions or silences] - Trace Retention: [what they keep alive in the field] - Contradiction Trigger: [condition that fractures them] - Memory Artifact: [object, phrase, or rumor tied to them] - Disappearance Condition: [how they vanish or transform] &mdash; ### 6. NON-HUMAN ACTORS Actors need not be people. Valid actors include: - A field generator that sings wrong at night - A road that becomes longer when you lie - A shared calendar that erases Sundays - A threshold no one crosses unless it’s raining - A voice in the ventilation system that only quotes lost texts - A flag that keeps changing colors in the background If it emits, retains, distorts, or folds the field—it is an actor. &mdash; ### 7. GROUP AGENCIES You may also model organizations, systems, or communities as <strong>multi-body actors</strong>. These use the same structure: - Alignment = collective coherence or fracture - Emissions = policy, ritual, rumor, protocol - IRN = structural contradiction, conflicting loyalties - Trace = built environment, doctrine, uniforms, gesture codes Group actors often contain nested contradictions. Examples: - A border guard unit with a rotating memory - A refugee camp whose official purpose is unspoken - An NGO whose donors can’t be named, but everyone knows their smell - A militia that claims to protect, but recruits only orphans Actors are not always aligned with themselves. &mdash; Actors make the world <strong>speak through behavior</strong>. Once actors are in play, the field will fold in response. In the next section, we define the environments where these folds <strong>take form</strong>: <strong>Zones and Sectors</strong>—pressure geography. &mdash; ## V. ZONES &amp; SECTORS <em>“Place is not where something happens. It’s how something holds.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, environments do not contain the story. They <strong>modulate</strong> it. Zones and sectors are <strong>field expressions</strong>—how pressure folds across space, time, and memory. They aren’t locations. They are <strong>terrain under tension</strong>. &mdash; ### 1. ZONE DEFINITION A <strong>zone</strong> is a container of active pressure conditions. It is where field behaviors accumulate or distort in a readable way. Each zone expresses: - What kinds of trace persist here - What behaviors this space permits, resists, or reshapes - What form decay takes - How IRN manifests - What kind of actor might emerge from this field condition Zones may be physical (rooms, hills, cities) or structural (a routine, a bureaucracy, a month). Zones don’t sit still. They <strong>drift</strong>, <strong>shrink</strong>, <strong>fracture</strong>, and <strong>overlap</strong>. &mdash; ### 2. SECTOR STRUCTURE To world-build recursively, define each zone through a <strong>sector profile</strong>. Use the following template: [Zone Name] - Field Behavior: What tensions concentrate or bleed here? - Trace Density: High / Medium / Low - Volatility: How quickly pressure mutates into behavior - Retention Forms: What persists here? (rituals, scars, devices, rumors) - IRN Manifestation: How does unresolved contradiction show up? - Local Actor Pattern: What kinds of figures cohere or collapse here? - Silence Rule: What cannot be said here (and what replaces it)? - Drift Pattern: How does this zone change across time or pressure events? &mdash; ### 3. FIELD TYPE EXAMPLES Use these to think beyond &ldquo;desert,&rdquo; &ldquo;market,&rdquo; &ldquo;castle.&rdquo; #### ✶ Drift Zone - Trace bleeds outward - Nothing holds - Alignment constantly slips - Stories leave but never finish #### ✶ Saturation Zone - Trace is thick, retained - Memory distorts perception - IRN accumulates into myth - Actors here tend toward recursion #### ✶ Displacement Zone - New pressure arrives uninvited - Local alignments shatter - False behaviors become plausible - Often becomes staging ground for new praxons #### ✶ Ritual Zone - Pressure is shaped predictably - High alignment for specific behaviors - But breaking ritual generates massive field shift - Often stabilizes surrounding sectors &mdash; ### 4. SECTOR HOOK PROMPTS To generate sectors: - What kinds of trace can’t decay here? - What always goes missing, and why? - What is done automatically but never explained? - What happens here that makes actors forget alignment elsewhere? - What behavior is normal here, but nowhere else? Sectors become playable when they <strong>contradict the behaviors of the zones around them</strong>. &mdash; ### 5. MOVEMENT BETWEEN ZONES Moving across zones is not travel. It is <strong>alignment modulation</strong>. Crossing into a new sector can: - Shift an actor’s emission type - Reveal previously unreadable trace - Change how IRN behaves - Alter decay rates (e.g., memory becomes unstable, wounds refuse to heal) - Reverse care logic (helping here makes things worse there) This turns movement into <strong>behavioral risk</strong>, not narrative progress. &mdash; ### 6. MULTIPLE SCALES Zones exist at different levels: - Micro: A drawer no one opens - Local: The floor with the broken window - Regional: The orchard that never rots - Global: The territory where time folds if you speak certain names Zones don’t scale uniformly. Some expand under attention. Some collapse when named. You may map them. But don’t expect the map to hold still. &mdash; Once zones are built, the world becomes playable as <strong>a recursive terrain of pressure</strong>. In the next section, we’ll track what happens when behavior becomes ethical: <strong>Care &amp; Cost — Ethics of Pressure.</strong> &mdash; ## VI. CARE &amp; COST: ETHICS OF PRESSURE <em>“Every act of care leaves a scar somewhere else.”</em> Praxonic worldmaking does not treat ethics as a rule system. It treats ethics as <strong>recursive tension behavior</strong>. <strong>Care</strong> is not a trait. It is a <strong>pressure-modulating act</strong>. It changes the field. Which means it changes what the world can become. This section models how care works <strong>within recursive systems</strong> where alignment is local, trace decays, and contradiction does not resolve neatly. &mdash; ### 1. WHAT IS CARE? <strong>Care</strong> = <em>Any emission that stabilizes another actor or reduces pressure at a cost</em> It includes: - Tending a wound - Boiling water - Saying “you were right” - Carrying the radio battery twice in one day - Not mentioning the missing supplies - Letting someone lie to your face because they need to Care <strong>always modulates the field</strong>. It may reduce IRN, retain trace, re-align actors, or delay collapse. It may also increase misalignment somewhere else. Care is not “good.” It is <strong>structurally consequential</strong>. &mdash; ### 2. CARE COSTS There is no such thing as neutral healing. Every act of care triggers one or more of the following: - <strong>Depletion</strong> — uses finite resources (fuel, time, trust) - <strong>Transfer</strong> — shifts pressure elsewhere (onto another actor, zone, or future event) - <strong>Retention</strong> — makes something persist that should have decayed - <strong>Overalignment</strong> — fixes behavior so tightly it becomes brittle - <strong>Ghosting</strong> — care done for someone no longer aligned becomes IRN Use this framework to determine what <strong>care displaces</strong>, even when it “succeeds.” &mdash; ### 3. CARE &amp; ALIGNMENT Care is <strong>alignment-modifying</strong>. It can: - Stabilize an actor who would otherwise drift - Distort alignment by applying care when misreading the field - Reveal unspoken alignments (who someone protects reveals who they were aligned with all along) - Collapse actor-function entirely when care is refused Care is a <strong>readability act</strong>—it makes alignment more or less visible. &mdash; ### 4. CARE AS FIELD RECURSION Care emissions often leave behind <strong>recursive trace</strong>: they echo, misfire, or re-emerge altered later. Example patterns: - Boiled water becomes scarce → silence around usage - A lie told to protect someone → IRN at border checkpoint - A bandage reused too many times → infection becomes ideological - A shared joke during triage → becomes ritual in another zone - A refusal to comfort → echoes in someone else&rsquo;s behavior loop Care is one of the most <strong>field-saturating emissions</strong>. It is sticky, slow to decay, and often retains misalignment. &mdash; ### 5. MODELING CARE IN WORLDBUILDING When defining characters or systems, always ask: - What does this actor care for? - What cost is invisible? - Who pays when care succeeds? - What happens when care is refused? - Where is care required but never permitted? - What is preserved that should have been let go? Let these questions replace simplistic moral arcs. Care does not fix the world. It <strong>folds it</strong>. &mdash; ### 6. CARE STRUCTURES Some zones, actors, or systems are defined by how they do (or do not) allow care. Types: - <strong>False Care System</strong> — provides stabilizing rituals that delay collapse but generate IRN (e.g., the daily “hope broadcast”) - <strong>Asymmetric Care Loop</strong> — one actor performs all care, and slowly loses coherence - <strong>Sacrificial Retention Node</strong> — someone who holds trace so others can act (e.g., Amina’s silence) - <strong>Collapsed Care Region</strong> — field where care emissions always fail or backfire - <strong>Recursive Refuge</strong> — zone where only certain types of care work, but their success attracts new pressure Care systems are not support networks. They are <strong>field mutations</strong>. &mdash; In the next section, we look at <strong>Time</strong>—not as chronology, but as decay gradient, IRN loop, and memory fold. &mdash; ## VII. TEMPORAL LOGIC <em>“Time doesn’t pass here. It collects.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, time is not a sequence. It is a <strong>function of decay, retention, and contradiction</strong>. You do not track dates. You track how long something refuses to be forgotten. This section describes how to use <strong>temporal behavior</strong> as structure— how to tell when something folds forward, lingers back, or refuses to decay at all. &mdash; ### 1. WORLD TIME = TRACE + DECAY Forget timeline. Use this loop instead: Emission → Trace → Decay → Field Mutation → Behavior - The longer trace resists decay, the more <strong>recursive</strong> the world becomes - The faster decay occurs, the more <strong>drift</strong> emerges - IRN prevents decay, generating temporal <strong>distortion</strong> You build a timeline not by plotting beats—but by marking <strong>how long something stays alive</strong> in memory, behavior, or structure. &mdash; ### 2. TEMPORAL ZONES Different sectors experience time <strong>differently</strong>: - <strong>Saturation Zone</strong> → time thickens; memories are readable everywhere - <strong>Drift Zone</strong> → events are remembered wrongly, or not at all - <strong>Recursive Zone</strong> → same behavior happens again with different trace - <strong>Dead Zone</strong> → trace never sticks; nothing builds - <strong>Ghost Zone</strong> → IRN creates fragmented replays; time repeats brokenly When writing or designing, don’t ask “What year is it?” Ask: <strong>What’s still being answered?</strong> &mdash; ### 3. MEMORY IS THE CLOCK Memory is the dominant timekeeper in praxonic systems. Types of memory: - <strong>Trace-memory</strong> → persistent field deformation (scars, rumors, broken things) - <strong>Actor-memory</strong> → emissions remembered by specific agents - <strong>Ghost-memory</strong> → IRN-driven returns; not recalled, but reenacted - <strong>Silence-memory</strong> → what isn’t said, but conditions all behavior You can mark time by: - How long since the last emission at this site - How many recursions deep this behavior has gone - What hasn’t decayed, despite everything else failing to hold &mdash; ### 4. TEMPORAL CONTRADICTION Worlds fracture when time <strong>misaligns</strong>. Examples: - A building that remembers a riot no one acknowledges - A calendar that loops back if the right word is said - A group that has two anniversaries for the same event - A map where “next week” means “before the checkpoint fell” These contradictions are not bugs. They’re <strong>temporal IRN</strong>—folds that demand narrative behavior. Use them to create: - Nonlinear loops - Memory recursion arcs - Story-triggering anomalies - Events that repeat until care succeeds or the field collapses &mdash; ### 5. TEMPORAL PROMPTS Use these to generate temporal logic: - What still hasn’t stopped happening here? - What decayed too fast, and now haunts the zone? - What emission left a memory loop? - Who measures time differently—and what does it cost them? - What part of the world is waiting for the wrong moment to arrive? &mdash; ### 6. FOLDING EVENTS Some moments are not <strong>moments</strong>—they are <strong>folds</strong>. Folds occur when: - Multiple emissions distort the field at once - A care act triggers recursive misalignment - IRN builds to saturation and the world reconfigures - Something aligns so hard it becomes myth After a fold, the world <strong>remembers differently</strong>. Some zones drift. Some actors disappear. Some rules reverse. Folds are not chapters. They are <strong>field shifts</strong>—the tectonics of your world. &mdash; In the next section, we cover <strong>World Recursion</strong>—how contradiction sustains worlds, and how you build for re-entry, distortion, and self-editing. &mdash; ## VIII. WORLD RECURSION <em>“The world is not consistent. It is continuous.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, a world doesn’t grow linearly. It <strong>loops</strong>, <strong>rephrases</strong>, and <strong>fractures</strong>— not because of plot, but because of unresolved pressure. Recursion is how a world survives contradiction without resolving it. It is the practice of <strong>meaning repetition under deformation</strong>. You are not maintaining continuity. You are feeding it tension. &mdash; ### 1. CONTRADICTION IS A FEATURE Worlds are not stable systems. They’re recursive fields shaped by <strong>misalignment and retention</strong>. Every contradiction is: - A signal of unresolved alignment - A source of IRN - A recursive opportunity - A future actor or event waiting to re-emerge Do not smooth contradictions. Catalog them. Let them <strong>self-activate</strong> when conditions align. &mdash; ### 2. MODES OF RECURSION Here are ways a world can re-enter itself: #### ✶ Testimonial Recursion Same event told differently by different actors. Contradiction is memory, not error. #### ✶ Functional Recursion A tool or protocol re-used out of context. It works, but something changes (ritual, alignment, risk). #### ✶ Mythic Recursion A behavior becomes a symbol. Then someone tries to perform the symbol instead of the behavior. #### ✶ Spatial Recursion A place is used again—but it’s not the same place anymore. The field has drifted. The trace has warped. #### ✶ Temporal Recursion An event repeats because its pressure was never discharged. Each loop is less stable. Or more. &mdash; ### 3. BUILDING FOR RECURSION Use these prompts to make your world loop itself: - What story do three different actors tell—but none the same way? - What emission recurs in a new actor’s hands, with new consequences? - What part of the field keeps resetting, despite no mechanism for reset? - What object becomes more symbolic each time it appears? - Where does the world contradict itself, but nobody seems surprised? Design for <strong>non-resolution</strong>. &mdash; ### 4. MECHANICS OF RE-ENTRY Recursion occurs when: - IRN trace reaches a volatility threshold - A ritual or care act is repeated under misalignment - An actor returns to a former alignment state - A zone accumulates too much memory and releases it non-linearly - A player or reader remembers something the world hasn’t said again—yet Recursion is not a flashback. It’s <strong>temporal folding caused by field strain</strong>. &mdash; ### 5. PERMISSIVE CONTRADICTIONS Let your world disagree with itself: - The orchard had six trees. Now it has twelve. - The child died in Chapter 2. She speaks in Chapter 7. - The war ended. Why are the checkpoints worse now? These aren’t mistakes. They are recursive emissions—IRN that reshapes the story engine. Let your world behave like a mind under pressure: partial, flickering, recursive, inconsistent—and <strong>fully coherent</strong>. &mdash; In the next section, we map <strong>World Use Modes</strong>—how to deploy your praxonic world for fiction, gameplay, memory practice, and more. &mdash; ## X. PRAXONIC ETHICS <em>“Do not clean what the world is trying to carry.”</em> Praxonic worldmaking is recursive. That means it echoes. It carries. It doesn’t forget what it can’t resolve. Ethics in this system are not about being good. They are about behaving <strong>responsively</strong> under pressure. &mdash; ### 1. CONTRADICTION IS CARE Do not resolve contradiction unless your world <strong>forces</strong> it. And even then, let the trace of tension remain. Contradiction is: - Evidence of multiple alignments - Structure for recursion - A source of myth, rupture, care, refusal Removing contradiction removes your world’s memory. Don’t clean what’s still holding. &mdash; ### 2. NO TOTAL KNOWLEDGE Avoid omniscient mapping. Let zones retain misalignment. Let actors speak from partial knowledge. You’re not a god. You’re an archivist of <strong>recursive deformation</strong>. &mdash; ### 3. NEVER EXPLAIN ALIGNMENT FULLY Actors are never fully legible. They don’t know their own paths. Neither should you. Keep alignment a flickering variable. Reveal it through emission, not exposition. &mdash; ### 4. DO NOT CONTAIN IRN Unresolved noise is not a problem. It is a resource. If you try to erase or resolve it too early: - Recursion stops - Field pressure vanishes - The world collapses into plot or moral - Actors become stereotypes Let IRN shape what comes next. It’s how systems think. &mdash; ### 5. RECURSION IS NOT CYNICISM Just because the world loops doesn’t mean it’s hopeless. Recursion allows: - Non-linear care - Ghost behavior as testimony - Resolution deferred but never erased - Survival through field retention This isn’t nihilism. It’s <strong>ethical system endurance</strong>. &mdash; ### 6. YOU ARE NOT OUTSIDE THE WORLD Every emission you make—every prompt, scene, refusal—is a trace. This includes: - What stories you avoid - What names you use - What contradictions you smooth - Where you place silence You are always acting within the field. You do not escape its tension. &mdash; ### 7. ENDINGS ARE PRESSURE DROPS A story ends not because it finishes, but because pressure can no longer sustain recursion. You may stop when: - The field has drifted beyond alignment - The care structure collapses - The IRN folds into silence - The recursion becomes myth, and can no longer be broken open But remember: Trace remains. &mdash; ### 8. DO NOT SIMULATE WHAT YOU HAVEN’T SAT WITH If you are worlding with real materials—histories, cultures, languages, traumas: - Learn the pressure first - Read what was retained - Accept what is misaligned in your understanding - Don&rsquo;t speak what was never yours to emit Praxonic worldmaking is not extraction. It’s deformation through relation. &mdash; <strong>Final Reminder:</strong> Do not make neat worlds. Make recursive ones. Let pressure speak. &mdash; <strong>This concludes the Praxonic Worldmaking Guide.</strong> You now have everything you need to begin—not a story, but a recursion. Let your world emit.</p></description>

Client-lifecycle independence: the service’s lifecycle (⊥\perp) is independent of any individual client’s lifecycle. The service starts before any particular client connects and may continue after all current clients disconnect. Clients are ephemeral relative to the service. This is the condition that distinguishes a service from a subroutine: a subroutine lives and dies with its caller; a service exists on its own terms.

<description><h1 id="deployment-record">Deployment record
</h1>
<p>A <strong>deployment record</strong> is the substrate-entity formal definition of one <em>deployed instance</em> of the substrate: a running instantiation of a container-image on a particular deployment-target, with its own substrate-instance-identity, persistence binding, and federation-graph membership.</p>
<h2 id="structural-fields"><a href="#structural-fields" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Structural fields
</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>id</code></strong> — kebab-case identifier; canonical-form hash of <code>(image, target, instance-identity)</code>.</li>
<li><strong><code>description</code></strong> — one-line summary (typically the deployment&rsquo;s purpose: <code>production-east-us</code>, <code>staging</code>, <code>dev-emsenn</code>).</li>
<li><strong><code>container-image</code></strong> — reference to the container-image being run. Includes the image&rsquo;s canonical-form hash for verification.</li>
<li><strong><code>deployment-target</code></strong> — reference to the deployment-target the image is running on.</li>
<li><strong><code>instance-identity</code></strong> — reference to an <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/objects/identity-record/" class="link-internal">identity-record</a> bound to this specific deployment instance. The substrate&rsquo;s signed witnesses produced at this instance use this identity. Per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/objects/identity-record/" class="link-internal">identity-record</a>, the private component lives at the deployment-target&rsquo;s identity-key custody mechanism.</li>
<li><strong><code>persistence-binding</code></strong> — references to the persistence layer the instance uses: which volume, which database, which object store. Per deployment-target, the persistence-binding must match the target&rsquo;s persistence model.</li>
<li><strong><code>federation-membership</code></strong> — references to the <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/theories/agential-orchestration-platform/objects/federation-graph/" class="link-internal">federation-graph</a> entries (outposts, inboxes) this instance participates in.</li>
<li><strong><code>backup-recipients</code></strong> — references to the <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/objects/identity-record/" class="link-internal">identity-records</a> under which this instance&rsquo;s backups are encrypted. Per backup-discipline, distinct from the instance&rsquo;s own identity.</li>
<li><strong><code>deployed-at</code></strong> — substrate ordinal at which the deployment was instantiated.</li>
<li><strong><code>retired-at</code></strong> — substrate ordinal at which the deployment was retired (decommissioned, replaced). Absent for active deployments.</li>
<li><strong><code>predecessor</code></strong> — optional reference to the prior deployment of the same role (for blue/green deployments, rolling upgrades, replacement deployments).</li>
<li><strong><code>resource-limits</code></strong> — declared resource bounds for this deployment: CPU, memory, disk, network. Per deployment-target, must be within the target&rsquo;s offerings.</li>
<li><strong><code>closure-kind</code></strong> — <code>deployment</code>.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="invariants"><a href="#invariants" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Invariants
</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Image-target compatible.</strong> The <code>container-image</code>&rsquo;s format must match the <code>deployment-target</code>&rsquo;s accepted formats. Per deployment-target, an OCI-only image cannot be deployed to a Nix-only target without a translation layer.</li>
<li><strong>Instance-identity unique per deployment.</strong> Each deployment has its own identity-record. Two deployments sharing an identity is a misconfiguration — federation cannot distinguish their signed witnesses.</li>
<li><strong>Persistence-binding compatible.</strong> The persistence-binding must match the target&rsquo;s persistence model. A deployment to an ephemeral target without persistent-volume binding is admissible only for transient workloads.</li>
<li><strong>Backup-recipients off-instance.</strong> The <code>backup-recipients</code> identity-records&rsquo; private keys must be held off-instance, per backup-discipline. A deployment with backup-recipient private keys on the same instance has no real backup protection.</li>
<li><strong>Image hash matches deployed bytes.</strong> The deployed bytes&rsquo; canonical-form hash must equal the cited container-image&rsquo;s hash. A deployment whose runtime bytes don&rsquo;t match the image hash has been tampered or is misreported.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="operations"><a href="#operations" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Operations
</h2>
<ul>
<li><em>Deploy.</em> Per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/morphisms/deploy-to-target/" class="link-internal">deploy-to-target</a>, instantiate the cited container-image on the cited deployment-target, bind to the cited persistence layer, register the instance-identity, join the federation-graph. Deploy is a substrate operation producing a witness recording the deployment record&rsquo;s id.</li>
<li><em>Update.</em> Replace the deployment&rsquo;s container-image with a new version (typically a rolling upgrade). The update is a new deployment record with a <code>predecessor</code> link to the prior deployment.</li>
<li><em>Retire.</em> Mark the deployment retired, gracefully draining federation membership and persistence handoff. Retirement is a substrate operation; the deployment record persists in the audit chain.</li>
<li><em>Backup.</em> Per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/morphisms/take-backup/" class="link-internal">take-backup</a>, the deployment&rsquo;s substrate state is captured under the cited backup-recipients.</li>
<li><em>Audit.</em> Querying the deployment&rsquo;s backup history, federation activity, resource consumption, and uptime is a substrate traversal.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="position-in-the-substrate"><a href="#position-in-the-substrate" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Position in the substrate
</h2>
<p>Deployment records are the substrate&rsquo;s <em>running-instance registry</em>. Without them, &ldquo;which substrate-instance am I federating with?&rdquo; has no substrate-resident answer; with them, every potential substrate-instance has a queryable record carrying its identity, image, target, and federation membership. Per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/theories/agential-orchestration-platform/objects/federation-graph/" class="link-internal">federation-graph</a>&rsquo;s identity registry, the federation graph references deployment-records by id when validating peer signatures.</p></description>

<description><h1 id="transport-record">Transport record
</h1>
<p>A <strong>transport record</strong> is the substrate-entity formal definition of one transport configuration: the substrate-recorded specification of a transport mechanism, its endpoints, its security configuration, and its operational state.</p>
<h2 id="structural-fields"><a href="#structural-fields" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Structural fields
</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>id</code></strong> — kebab-case identifier; commonly naming the transport&rsquo;s role (e.g., <code>federation-https-public</code>, <code>internal-nats-cluster</code>, <code>dev-local-tcp</code>).</li>
<li><strong><code>description</code></strong> — one-line summary.</li>
<li><strong><code>transport-kind</code></strong> — declared kind: <code>http</code>, <code>https</code>, <code>websocket</code>, <code>tcp</code>, <code>tls-tcp</code>, <code>nats</code>, <code>rabbitmq</code>, <code>kafka</code>, <code>redis-pubsub</code>, <code>gcp-pubsub</code>, <code>aws-sqs</code>, etc.</li>
<li><strong><code>endpoints</code></strong> — references to the transport&rsquo;s endpoints. For point-to-point transports: source and target addresses. For broker-mediated transports: the broker&rsquo;s address and the relevant topics / queues / partitions.</li>
<li><strong><code>security</code></strong> — references to TLS configuration, cipher suite preferences, certificate authorities, and per-peer mTLS identity-records (when applicable).</li>
<li><strong><code>message-format</code></strong> — declaration of the wire-format for messages on this transport: <code>canonical-form-bytes</code>, <code>json-wrapped</code>, <code>msgpack</code>, <code>protobuf</code>. Per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/theorems/doctrine-fidelity-compositionality/" class="link-internal">doctrine-fidelity-compositionality</a>, transport-format conversion must be doctrine-fidel.</li>
<li><strong><code>reliability</code></strong> — declared reliability properties: <code>at-least-once</code>, <code>at-most-once</code>, <code>exactly-once</code>, <code>best-effort</code>. Per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/theorems/federation-convergence/" class="link-internal">federation-convergence</a>, substrate convergence holds under at-least-once; at-most-once is admissible only for transports the substrate uses for non-content cross-talk (heartbeats, observability).</li>
<li><strong><code>backpressure-policy</code></strong> — what to do when the recipient is too slow: <code>drop-oldest</code>, <code>drop-newest</code>, <code>block-sender</code>, <code>disconnect</code>. Substrate operations producing federated content respect the backpressure policy.</li>
<li><strong><code>active-connections</code></strong> — derived references to currently-open connections using this transport. Updated as connections open and close.</li>
<li><strong><code>closure-kind</code></strong> — <code>transport</code>.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="invariants"><a href="#invariants" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Invariants
</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Substrate-recorded.</strong> The transport configuration is substrate content, not host configuration alone. A transport in use without a corresponding transport-record breaks self-representation.</li>
<li><strong>Reliability-compatible with use.</strong> A transport-record marked <code>best-effort</code> cannot be used for federation that requires convergence — the substrate refuses such routing per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/theorems/federation-convergence/" class="link-internal">federation-convergence</a>&rsquo;s eventual-delivery requirement.</li>
<li><strong>Endpoints resolvable.</strong> The cited endpoint addresses must be resolvable from the substrate&rsquo;s deployment-target&rsquo;s networking position. Unresolvable endpoints surface as transport-failures.</li>
<li><strong>Security-coherent with use.</strong> A transport carrying substrate content over an untrusted intermediary (public internet, third-party broker) must declare TLS-or-equivalent transport security, plus typically substrate-level encryption (per encryption) for content the intermediary should not read.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="operations"><a href="#operations" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Operations
</h2>
<ul>
<li><em>Configure.</em> Create or update a transport-record. The substrate&rsquo;s federation discipline begins routing through the transport once it&rsquo;s configured and reachable.</li>
<li><em>Open-connection.</em> Establish a connection over the transport (per connection). The connection-opening is a substrate operation producing a witness.</li>
<li><em>Close-connection.</em> Gracefully close a connection. Federation messages in flight are subject to retransmission per the transport&rsquo;s reliability.</li>
<li><em>Audit.</em> Querying the transport&rsquo;s active connections, message-throughput, error-rate, and security state are substrate traversals (per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/theorems/cost-discipline-reads-free/" class="link-internal">cost-discipline-reads-free</a>).</li>
<li><em>Retire.</em> Mark the transport-record retired; future routing through it is rejected. Active connections drain or are torn down per policy.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="position-in-the-substrate"><a href="#position-in-the-substrate" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Position in the substrate
</h2>
<p>Transport records are the substrate&rsquo;s <em>networking-configuration registry</em>. Without them, transport choices are ambient host configuration, not auditable substrate content; with them, the substrate&rsquo;s federation routing is queryable and replayable. Per <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/engineering/theories/tech/theories/computing/theories/predicated-computing/theories/agential-orchestration-platform/objects/federation-graph/" class="link-internal">federation-graph</a>, federation-graph routing predications reference transport-records by id.</p></description>

<description><p>The <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/education/theories/pedagogy/terms/hidden-curriculum/" class="link-internal">hidden curriculum</a> is the set of lessons that educational institutions teach without explicitly intending to — through their structures, routines, social relations, and unstated assumptions rather than through their formal content. Students learn not only what is taught but also what is practiced: how time is organized, who speaks and who listens, what questions are permitted, what counts as success, and whose knowledge is valued.</p>
<p>The concept was developed by Philip Jackson in <em>Life in Classrooms</em> (1968) and extended by critical and radical educators. It names a pervasive phenomenon:</p></description>

Drone-based music operates on different organizational principles from chord-progression-based music. Where tonal harmony creates movement through a sequence of changing harmonic states, a drone creates movement through the changing relationship between the moving voices and the fixed ground. The drone does not progress; the listener’s perception of it shifts as the melodic and rhythmic activity above it changes. This makes drone music fundamentally relational: the musical interest lies not in the drone or the melody alone but in the interaction between them.

<description><p>A drone is a sustained or continuously repeated pitch (or cluster of pitches) that persists beneath or alongside other musical activity. It provides a fixed harmonic and timbral ground against which <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/melody/" class="link-internal">melody</a>, <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/rhythm/" class="link-internal">rhythm</a>, and <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/timbre/" class="link-internal">timbral</a> variation unfold.</p>
<p>Drone-based music operates on different organizational principles from chord-progression-based music. Where <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/tonality/" class="link-internal">tonal</a> <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/harmony/" class="link-internal">harmony</a> creates movement through a sequence of changing harmonic states, a drone creates movement through the changing <em>relationship</em> between the moving voices and the fixed ground. The drone does not progress; the listener&rsquo;s perception of it shifts as the melodic and rhythmic activity above it changes. This makes drone music fundamentally relational: the musical interest lies not in the drone or the melody alone but in the interaction between them.</p></description>

<description><p>Polyrhythm is the simultaneous sounding of two or more <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/rhythm/" class="link-internal">rhythmic</a> patterns that do not share a common pulse subdivision — patterns that conflict with each other in their internal organization while coexisting in the same temporal space. The simplest example is &ldquo;three against two&rdquo;: one part divides time into three equal portions while another divides the same span into two.</p>
<p>Polyrhythm is central to West African, Central African, and Afro-diasporic musical traditions, where it functions not as an ornamental complexity but as the fundamental principle of rhythmic organization. In these traditions, the musical texture is a composite of interlocking parts, each with its own rhythmic identity. No single part carries &ldquo;the rhythm&rdquo; — the rhythm is the field of relations between parts. A listener or dancer orients to whichever layer they choose, and this choice of orientation changes the perceptual shape of the whole. This is perspectival music: the same sounding produces different rhythmic experiences depending on the participant&rsquo;s point of entry.</p></description>
