The word “harmony” carries a normative connotation that is worth noting: it implies agreement, concord, things fitting together properly. This connotation has been used ideologically — to naturalize particular social arrangements as “harmonious” and to frame dissonance (musical or social) as disorder. A relational approach to harmony treats consonance and dissonance not as natural categories but as culturally constituted relations: what sounds “resolved” depends on what the listener has learned to expect.

<description><p>Consonance is the perceptual quality of stability, rest, or &ldquo;fitting together&rdquo; in a combination of simultaneous pitches. Its complement is <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/dissonance/" class="link-internal">dissonance</a> — the quality of tension, roughness, or instability. Together, consonance and <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/dissonance/" class="link-internal">dissonance</a> form the basic polarity of <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/harmony/" class="link-internal">harmonic</a> perception in the Western theoretical tradition.</p>
<p>The distinction between consonance and dissonance has been explained in acoustical terms (ratios of frequencies, coincidence of overtones), psychoacoustical terms (roughness, beating), and cultural terms (learned expectations, stylistic convention). No single explanation is sufficient. Intervals classified as dissonant in medieval European theory (the third) became the foundation of consonance in Renaissance practice. What counts as &ldquo;resolved&rdquo; or &ldquo;at rest&rdquo; is shaped by the listener&rsquo;s training, tradition, and the musical context.</p></description>

<description><p>Dissonance is the perceptual quality of tension, roughness, or instability in a combination of simultaneous pitches. In Western tonal practice, dissonance creates the drive toward resolution — the expectation that tension will give way to <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/consonance/" class="link-internal">consonance</a>. Without dissonance, tonal music would have no motion; it is the engine of <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/harmony/" class="link-internal">harmonic</a> movement.</p>
<p>Like <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/consonance/" class="link-internal">consonance</a>, dissonance is not a fixed property of intervals but a culturally and contextually shaped perception. What sounds dissonant depends on what the listener expects, and expectations are trained by exposure to particular musical systems. The history of Western music can be read as a progressive expansion of the boundary between consonance and dissonance: intervals that sounded harsh in one century became unremarkable in the next.</p></description>

<description><p>Melody is a sequence of pitches perceived as a single coherent line — a movement through pitch space that has direction, contour, and shape. It is what most people mean when they say they have a song &ldquo;stuck in their head&rdquo;: the singable part, the line that carries identity.</p>
<p>A melody is not simply a series of notes. It is a <em>gestalt</em>: the listener perceives it as a whole with internal logic, not as a collection of isolated pitches. This perception depends on <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/rhythm/" class="link-internal">rhythm</a> (the durations and accents that give the pitch sequence its shape), on contour (the pattern of ascending and descending motion), and on the melodic conventions of the listener&rsquo;s musical culture. A phrase that sounds like a coherent melody in one tradition may sound like arbitrary pitches in another.</p></description>

<description><p>Rhythm is the organization of sound in time. It is the most fundamental musical parameter — you can have music without <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/melody/" class="link-internal">melody</a> or <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/harmony/" class="link-internal">harmony</a>, but you cannot have music without temporal structure. Rhythm is what makes sound <em>move</em>.</p>
<p>At its simplest, rhythm is a pattern of durations: long and short, stressed and unstressed, sounded and silent. But rhythm is not merely a property of the sound itself. It is a relation between the sound and the body that perceives it. A rhythm exists in the interaction between acoustic pattern and embodied expectation — the listener&rsquo;s sense of where the next beat will fall, whether it arrives early, late, or not at all. This is why rhythm moves people physically: it entrains bodily processes (breathing, walking, heartbeat) into its temporal field.</p></description>

<description><p>Timbre is the quality of a sound — what makes a flute sound different from a violin playing the same note at the same volume. It is sometimes called &ldquo;tone color,&rdquo; and like color, it is easier to perceive than to describe. Western music theory has historically had little vocabulary for timbre compared to its elaborate systems for <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/rhythm/" class="link-internal">rhythm</a>, <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/melody/" class="link-internal">melody</a>, and <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/music/theories/music-theory/terms/harmony/" class="link-internal">harmony</a>.</p>
<p>Acoustically, timbre arises from the spectral content of a sound: the relative amplitudes and frequencies of the overtones that accompany the fundamental pitch, the way those overtones change over time (the &ldquo;envelope&rdquo;), and the noise components mixed in. But timbre is not reducible to a spectrum. It is a perceptual category — the listener&rsquo;s synthesis of multiple acoustic dimensions into a single qualitative impression.</p></description>

A melody is not simply a series of notes. It is a gestalt: the listener perceives it as a whole with internal logic, not as a collection of isolated pitches. This perception depends on rhythm (the durations and accents that give the pitch sequence its shape), on contour (the pattern of ascending and descending motion), and on the melodic conventions of the listener’s musical culture. A phrase that sounds like a coherent melody in one tradition may sound like arbitrary pitches in another.

Not all music is metered. Free-rhythm performance (the alap in Hindustani classical music, recitative in opera, many forms of chant) organizes time without a recurring pulse pattern. And in many polyrhythmic traditions, the concept of a single governing meter is inadequate — the music sustains multiple metric frameworks simultaneously, and the listener’s sense of “where the beat falls” depends on which layer they attend to.

At its simplest, rhythm is a pattern of durations: long and short, stressed and unstressed, sounded and silent. But rhythm is not merely a property of the sound itself. It is a relation between the sound and the body that perceives it. A rhythm exists in the interaction between acoustic pattern and embodied expectation — the listener’s sense of where the next beat will fall, whether it arrives early, late, or not at all. This is why rhythm moves people physically: it entrains bodily processes (breathing, walking, heartbeat) into its temporal field.

In many African and Afro-diasporic musical traditions, rhythm is not a subordinate parameter serving melody but the primary organizing force. Polyrhythm — the layering of multiple independent rhythmic patterns — creates a relational field in which no single pattern is “the rhythm.” The rhythm is the interaction between patterns, and each listener or dancer may orient to a different layer. This makes rhythm a collective, perspectival phenomenon rather than a single objective structure.

Acoustically, timbre arises from the spectral content of a sound: the relative amplitudes and frequencies of the overtones that accompany the fundamental pitch, the way those overtones change over time (the “envelope”), and the noise components mixed in. But timbre is not reducible to a spectrum. It is a perceptual category — the listener’s synthesis of multiple acoustic dimensions into a single qualitative impression.

Process view: A conversation IS the exchange itself. It exists only in the moment-to-moment flow of speech, listening, response. Each participant is continuously creating their contribution based on what they hear; each speaker shapes what comes next in the exchange. The conversation has no fixed identity apart from this unfolding process. It is constituted by the mutual attention and responsiveness of the participants—stop that, and the conversation ceases to exist, even if the same people remain in the same room.

• Fiction opens with a situation that implies instability — a character who wants something, a world that’s about to change, a voice so compelling the reader wants to keep listening. The first line of a novel carries disproportionate weight because it’s the reader’s first encounter with the voice and world.

<description><p>A <em><strong>hook</strong></em> is an opening that gives the reader a reason to keep reading. The term comes from journalism (where the opening is called the <strong>lede</strong>) but applies across all writing: the first sentence, paragraph, or page must earn the reader&rsquo;s attention, because no one is obligated to finish what they started.</p>
<p>Different genres hook in different ways:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Journalism</strong> opens with the most important information — who, what, when, where, why — because readers may stop at any point and should leave with the essential facts.</li>
<li><strong>Essays</strong> often open with a concrete scene, a surprising fact, a question, or a provocative claim — something that creates enough curiosity or tension to pull the reader into the argument.</li>
<li><strong>Fiction</strong> opens with a situation that implies instability — a <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/writing/theories/fiction/terms/character/" class="link-internal">character</a> who wants something, a world that&rsquo;s about to change, a voice so compelling the reader wants to keep listening. The first line of a novel carries disproportionate weight because it&rsquo;s the reader&rsquo;s first encounter with the <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/writing/theories/rhetoric-and-composition/terms/voice/" class="link-internal">voice</a> and world.</li>
<li><strong>Technical writing</strong> opens with context: what is this document about, who is it for, and why should they read it. The hook is relevance — &ldquo;this will help you do something you need to do.&rdquo;</li>
</ul>
<p>The common mistake is opening with background, definitions, or a history of the topic. These are legitimate content but poor hooks — they ask the reader to wade through context before encountering anything they care about. The stronger move is to start with the thing the reader cares about and provide context as needed.</p></description>

<description><p><em><strong>Protocol-aided audience analysis</strong></em> is <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/references/people/karen-schriver/" class="link-internal">Karen Schriver</a>&rsquo;s method of using <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/writing/theories/plain-language/terms/think-aloud-protocol/" class="link-internal">think-aloud protocols</a> to study how real readers process documents — watching and listening as they read, noting where they hesitate, misread, backtrack, or give up [@schriver1997].</p>
<p>Schriver distinguished three approaches to <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/business/terms/audience/" class="link-internal">audience</a> analysis:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong>Classification-based</strong> — assigning demographic categories (age, education, job role). This is the easiest and least useful: knowing that readers are &ldquo;college-educated adults&rdquo; doesn&rsquo;t reveal what they&rsquo;ll misunderstand.</li>
<li><strong>Intuition-based</strong> — the writer imagines a reader and predicts their responses. This is better but unreliable: Schriver&rsquo;s research showed that writers systematically overestimate how well readers understand their text.</li>
<li><strong>Feedback-based</strong> — observing real readers using the document. Protocol-aided audience analysis is the most rigorous form of feedback-based analysis.</li>
</ol>
<p>In a protocol-aided session, a reader thinks aloud while using a document to accomplish a task. The writer (or researcher) observes without helping, recording where comprehension breaks down. The resulting data reveals problems that classification and intuition can&rsquo;t detect: a heading that misleads, a paragraph that readers skip, a term that readers misinterpret.</p></description>

<description><p>Meter is the abstract pattern that a metrical poem keeps a near-bargain with — a fixed template of stressed and unstressed syllables, of syllable counts, or of long and short syllables, against which each spoken line is heard.
The word comes from Greek <em>métron</em> (&ldquo;measure&rdquo;), and the measuring is the point: a metrical line is one whose ear-shape has been counted in advance.</p>
<p>Meter does not live on the page.
It lives in the listener.
A line of iambic pentameter does not become metrical because a poet has typed ten syllables; it becomes metrical because a reader who knows the pattern hears each syllable land on or off the beat the pattern predicts.
The poem and the reader together perform the meter — the poem proposes it, the reader carries it, and the spoken line either fulfills, delays, or breaks it.
This is why meter has expressive force.
A line that meets the pattern exactly <em>settles</em> into it; a line that violates the pattern <em>registers as violation</em> only because the pattern is already in the ear.</p></description>

<description><h2 id="assumed-audience"><a href="#assumed-audience" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Assumed audience
</h2>
<ul>
<li>Reading level: comfortable with prose; willing to read poems aloud and listen to them.</li>
<li>Background: has read <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/writing/theories/poetry/texts/the-line-and-the-break/" class="link-internal">The Line and the Break</a> or otherwise understands the line as poetry&rsquo;s basic unit.</li>
<li>Goal: hear what makes a poem metrical, recognize the major metrical systems, and understand what metrical poetry does that free verse does not.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="a-poem-is-metrical-when-its-line-keeps-a-bargain"><a href="#a-poem-is-metrical-when-its-line-keeps-a-bargain" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>A poem is metrical when its line keeps a bargain
</h2>
<p>A metrical poem is one whose lines have been counted in advance.
Before the poet begins, a pattern has been chosen — a number of stresses, a number of syllables, a fixed alternation of stressed and unstressed — and each line is written to keep a near-bargain with that pattern.
The reader, hearing the first few lines, learns the pattern.
After that, every line lands either inside the pattern, just outside it, or against it, and each landing has expressive force.</p></description>

Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi belong to the Glomeromycota, an ancient fungal phylum that associates with over 80% of land plant species. They are obligate symbionts — unable to grow without a plant host — and they produce no conspicuous fruiting bodies. Their reproduction and dispersal depend on large, thick-walled spores produced in the soil. The arbuscule itself is ephemeral: individual arbuscules are produced, function for days to weeks, then collapse and are digested by the plant cell, which may then be recolonized by a new arbuscule. This cycle of formation, function, and collapse is continuous throughout the life of the mycorrhizal association.

The theory applies whenever perfect reproduction is unnecessary or impractical. Speech, images, and video all contain more detail than a listener or viewer can distinguish, so discarding some of that detail in a principled way allows dramatic reductions in data rate without perceptible loss.

<description><p>The musculoskeletal system provides structural support, enables movement, and protects internal organs. It consists of bones (the skeleton), skeletal muscles (the motors), and the connective <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/science/theories/medicine/theories/human-body/terms/tissue/" class="link-internal">tissues</a> that link them (tendons, ligaments, cartilage, fascia). This is the organ system that somatics works with most directly — and the system whose dysfunction produces a significant proportion of <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/science/theories/medicine/theories/pain/terms/chronic-pain/" class="link-internal">chronic pain</a>.</p>
<h2 id="bones"><a href="#bones" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Bones
</h2>
<p>The human skeleton contains 206 bones. Bones provide:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Structural support</strong> — the rigid framework that holds the body upright against gravity</li>
<li><strong>Protection</strong> — the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs, the vertebral column protects the spinal cord</li>
<li><strong>Movement</strong> — bones serve as levers that muscles pull on to produce movement</li>
<li><strong>Mineral storage</strong> — bones store calcium and phosphorus, releasing them into the blood as needed</li>
<li><strong>Blood cell production</strong> — red bone marrow (inside certain bones) produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets</li>
</ul>
<p>Bones meet at <strong>joints</strong> — the points of articulation that determine the range and type of movement possible. Joint types include hinge joints (elbow, knee), ball-and-socket joints (hip, shoulder), pivot joints (atlas-axis at the top of the spine), and gliding joints (wrist, ankle). The range of motion at a joint is determined by the bone shapes, the ligaments (connective tissue bands connecting bone to bone), and the tone of the muscles crossing the joint.</p></description>

<description><h2 id="what-you-will-be-able-to-do"><a href="#what-you-will-be-able-to-do" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>What you will be able to do
</h2>
<ul>
<li>Explain why pain is an output of the nervous system rather than a direct readout of tissue damage, and why this distinction matters clinically.</li>
<li>Identify the three domains of the biopsychosocial model (biological, psychological, social) and give examples of how each contributes to a pain presentation.</li>
<li>Describe how psychological factors — particularly catastrophizing, fear-avoidance, and trauma history — influence pain through descending modulation and central sensitization, not as separate &ldquo;mental&rdquo; processes.</li>
<li>Recognize when a pain presentation cannot be explained by the biomedical model alone (e.g., pain without tissue damage, normal imaging with severe pain, pain that persists long after healing).</li>
<li>Analyze a chronic pain scenario by identifying biological contributors (nociception, sensitization, deconditioning), psychological contributors (beliefs, affect, coping patterns), and social contributors (clinical interactions, structural conditions, access to care).</li>
<li>Explain how the clinical relationship itself — what the clinician says, how they listen, whether they validate the patient&rsquo;s experience — affects pain through the same neural mechanisms as any other intervention.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="prerequisites"><a href="#prerequisites" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Prerequisites
</h2>
<ul>
<li>Familiarity with basic neurophysiology is helpful but not required — the introductory curriculum covers the necessary foundations.</li>
<li>No clinical experience required. The skill is designed for anyone encountering pain science for the first time.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="reference-documents"><a href="#reference-documents" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Reference documents
</h2>

How pain is assessed affects pain itself. A clinician who listens carefully, takes the report seriously, explains the mechanisms, and communicates a plan activates the patient’s sense of being understood — which, through descending modulation and therapeutic alliance effects, can itself reduce pain. A clinician who rushes through the assessment, expresses skepticism, or attributes pain to psychological causes without explanation produces the opposite effect: threat perception increases, descending modulation shifts toward facilitation, and pain amplifies.

Based on the psychodynamic tradition. Focuses on unconscious patterns, defense mechanisms, and the therapeutic relationship as the site of change. The therapist listens for what is not said as much as what is said — for the gaps, contradictions, and emotional shifts that signal unconscious material. Interpretations (the therapist’s observations about patterns) are offered tentatively, as hypotheses to be explored rather than truths to be accepted.

Based on the humanistic tradition. Less structured than CBT, more focused on the client’s subjective experience and the quality of the therapeutic encounter. The therapist’s primary tools are empathic listening, unconditional positive regard, and authenticity.
• A confiding relationship — having someone who listens without judgment, who is reliably present, and who holds information in confidence

<description><p>The musculoskeletal system provides structural support, enables movement, and protects internal organs. It consists of bones (the skeleton), skeletal muscles (the motors), and the connective <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/science/theories/medicine/theories/human-body/terms/tissue/" class="link-internal">tissues</a> that link them (tendons, ligaments, cartilage, fascia). This is the organ system that somatics works with most directly — and the system whose dysfunction produces a significant proportion of <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/science/theories/medicine/theories/pain/terms/chronic-pain/" class="link-internal">chronic pain</a>.</p>
<h2 id="bones"><a href="#bones" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Bones
</h2>
<p>The human skeleton contains 206 bones. Bones provide:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Structural support</strong> — the rigid framework that holds the body upright against gravity</li>
<li><strong>Protection</strong> — the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs, the vertebral column protects the spinal cord</li>
<li><strong>Movement</strong> — bones serve as levers that muscles pull on to produce movement</li>
<li><strong>Mineral storage</strong> — bones store calcium and phosphorus, releasing them into the blood as needed</li>
<li><strong>Blood cell production</strong> — red bone marrow (inside certain bones) produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets</li>
</ul>
<p>Bones meet at <strong>joints</strong> — the points of articulation that determine the range and type of movement possible. Joint types include hinge joints (elbow, knee), ball-and-socket joints (hip, shoulder), pivot joints (atlas-axis at the top of the spine), and gliding joints (wrist, ankle). The range of motion at a joint is determined by the bone shapes, the ligaments (connective tissue bands connecting bone to bone), and the tone of the muscles crossing the joint.</p></description>

<h2 id="subscription-versus-membership"><a href="#subscription-versus-membership" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Subscription versus membership
</h2>
<p>These terms are often used interchangeably, but they describe different value propositions.</p>
<p>A <strong>subscription</strong> is a payment for access to content. The subscriber pays to read, watch, or listen to material that non-subscribers cannot access. The value proposition is the content itself. The New York Times, The Information, and most paywalled publications are subscription businesses. If the content stopped being published, the reason to subscribe would disappear.</p></description>

<description><p>The <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/education/theories/pedagogy/terms/hidden-curriculum/" class="link-internal">hidden curriculum</a> is the set of lessons that educational institutions teach without explicitly intending to — through their structures, routines, social relations, and unstated assumptions rather than through their formal content. Students learn not only what is taught but also what is practiced: how time is organized, who speaks and who listens, what questions are permitted, what counts as success, and whose knowledge is valued.</p>
<p>The concept was developed by Philip Jackson in <em>Life in Classrooms</em> (1968) and extended by critical and radical educators. It names a pervasive phenomenon:</p></description>

<description><p><a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/education/theories/knowledge-transmission/terms/oral-transmission/" class="link-internal">Oral transmission</a> is the carrying of knowledge through speech, story, song, chant, proverb, and spoken instruction — without dependence on textual inscription. It is the oldest and most widespread mode of knowledge transmission, practiced by every human culture and still primary in many.</p>
<p>Oral transmission is not a deficiency. It is a mode with specific capabilities that text lacks:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Contextual adaptation.</strong> The storyteller adjusts the telling to the audience, the situation, the season, the purpose. The &ldquo;same&rdquo; story told to children and to elders carries different knowledge. This adaptability is a feature, not a limitation — it keeps knowledge alive and responsive rather than frozen.</li>
<li><strong>Relational embedding.</strong> Oral knowledge is transmitted in relationship — between speaker and listener, between elder and youth, between the living and the ancestors whose words are carried forward. The relationship is part of the knowledge: who tells, who listens, and under what conditions matters.</li>
<li><strong>Mnemonic structure.</strong> Oral traditions develop sophisticated mnemonic devices — rhythm, rhyme, repetition, formulaic phrases, narrative structure, musical form — that enable faithful transmission across generations without writing. These structures are not primitive substitutes for literacy; they are technologies of memory with their own rigor.</li>
<li><strong>Embodied presence.</strong> Oral transmission requires the presence of the speaker — their voice, gesture, expression, breath. Knowledge carried in these dimensions is lost when reduced to transcript.</li>
</ul>
<p>Oral transmission is primary in Indigenous pedagogies, where storytelling, ceremony, and mentorship are the principal modes of education. It is central to Black radical pedagogies, where the sermon, the testimony, the freedom song, and the study circle carry knowledge that written archives cannot hold. It is present in non-Western pedagogies — the ubuntu tradition, Buddhist oral lineages, Islamic <em>halqa</em> study circles.</p></description>

<description><h2 id="assumed-audience"><a href="#assumed-audience" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Assumed audience
</h2>
<ul>
<li>Reading level: comfortable with prose; willing to read poems aloud and listen to them.</li>
<li>Background: has read <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/writing/theories/poetry/texts/the-line-and-the-break/" class="link-internal">The Line and the Break</a> or otherwise understands the line as poetry&rsquo;s basic unit.</li>
<li>Goal: hear what makes a poem metrical, recognize the major metrical systems, and understand what metrical poetry does that free verse does not.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="a-poem-is-metrical-when-its-line-keeps-a-bargain"><a href="#a-poem-is-metrical-when-its-line-keeps-a-bargain" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>A poem is metrical when its line keeps a bargain
</h2>
<p>A metrical poem is one whose lines have been counted in advance.
Before the poet begins, a pattern has been chosen — a number of stresses, a number of syllables, a fixed alternation of stressed and unstressed — and each line is written to keep a near-bargain with that pattern.
The reader, hearing the first few lines, learns the pattern.
After that, every line lands either inside the pattern, just outside it, or against it, and each landing has expressive force.</p></description>

<description><h2 id="what-you-will-be-able-to-do"><a href="#what-you-will-be-able-to-do" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>What you will be able to do
</h2>
<ul>
<li>Explain why pain is an output of the nervous system rather than a direct readout of tissue damage, and why this distinction matters clinically.</li>
<li>Identify the three domains of the biopsychosocial model (biological, psychological, social) and give examples of how each contributes to a pain presentation.</li>
<li>Describe how psychological factors — particularly catastrophizing, fear-avoidance, and trauma history — influence pain through descending modulation and central sensitization, not as separate &ldquo;mental&rdquo; processes.</li>
<li>Recognize when a pain presentation cannot be explained by the biomedical model alone (e.g., pain without tissue damage, normal imaging with severe pain, pain that persists long after healing).</li>
<li>Analyze a chronic pain scenario by identifying biological contributors (nociception, sensitization, deconditioning), psychological contributors (beliefs, affect, coping patterns), and social contributors (clinical interactions, structural conditions, access to care).</li>
<li>Explain how the clinical relationship itself — what the clinician says, how they listen, whether they validate the patient&rsquo;s experience — affects pain through the same neural mechanisms as any other intervention.</li>
</ul>

</h2>
<ul>
<li>Familiarity with basic neurophysiology is helpful but not required — the introductory curriculum covers the necessary foundations.</li>
<li>No clinical experience required. The skill is designed for anyone encountering pain science for the first time.</li>
</ul>

<description><p>The musculoskeletal system provides structural support, enables movement, and protects internal organs. It consists of bones (the skeleton), skeletal muscles (the motors), and the connective <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/science/theories/medicine/theories/human-body/terms/tissue/" class="link-internal">tissues</a> that link them (tendons, ligaments, cartilage, fascia). This is the organ system that somatics works with most directly — and the system whose dysfunction produces a significant proportion of <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/science/theories/medicine/theories/pain/terms/chronic-pain/" class="link-internal">chronic pain</a>.</p>
<h2 id="bones"><a href="#bones" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Bones
</h2>
<p>The human skeleton contains 206 bones. Bones provide:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Structural support</strong> — the rigid framework that holds the body upright against gravity</li>
<li><strong>Protection</strong> — the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs, the vertebral column protects the spinal cord</li>
<li><strong>Movement</strong> — bones serve as levers that muscles pull on to produce movement</li>
<li><strong>Mineral storage</strong> — bones store calcium and phosphorus, releasing them into the blood as needed</li>
<li><strong>Blood cell production</strong> — red bone marrow (inside certain bones) produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets</li>
</ul>
<p>Bones meet at <strong>joints</strong> — the points of articulation that determine the range and type of movement possible. Joint types include hinge joints (elbow, knee), ball-and-socket joints (hip, shoulder), pivot joints (atlas-axis at the top of the spine), and gliding joints (wrist, ankle). The range of motion at a joint is determined by the bone shapes, the ligaments (connective tissue bands connecting bone to bone), and the tone of the muscles crossing the joint.</p></description>

</h2>
<ul>

<li>Background: has read <a href="https://emsenn.net/library/theories/humanities/theories/writing/theories/poetry/texts/the-line-and-the-break/" class="link-internal">The Line and the Break</a> or otherwise understands the line as poetry&rsquo;s basic unit.</li>
<li>Goal: hear what makes a poem metrical, recognize the major metrical systems, and understand what metrical poetry does that free verse does not.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="a-poem-is-metrical-when-its-line-keeps-a-bargain"><a href="#a-poem-is-metrical-when-its-line-keeps-a-bargain" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>A poem is metrical when its line keeps a bargain
</h2>
<p>A metrical poem is one whose lines have been counted in advance.
Before the poet begins, a pattern has been chosen — a number of stresses, a number of syllables, a fixed alternation of stressed and unstressed — and each line is written to keep a near-bargain with that pattern.
The reader, hearing the first few lines, learns the pattern.
After that, every line lands either inside the pattern, just outside it, or against it, and each landing has expressive force.</p></description>

<description><p>Emergent disaster response relies on a recurring cluster of practices.
Across storms, floods, and pandemics, grassroots groups repeatedly use
local needs assessment, decentralized volunteer intake, improvised
logistics, hub-based distribution, peer communication, and adaptive
resource routing rather than fixed top-down workflows [@ambinder2013;
@twiggmosel2017; @knearem2024].</p>
<h2 id="direct-listening-and-local-needs-assessment"><a href="#direct-listening-and-local-needs-assessment" class="heading-anchor" aria-label="Link to this section">¶</a>Direct listening and local needs assessment
</h2>
<p>Groups begin by asking affected people what they need and then updating
those answers as conditions change. Common Ground&rsquo;s early work in New
Orleans and later mutual-aid networks during COVID both relied on this
practice rather than treating need as something fully knowable from a
distance [@commonground2024; @knearem2024].</p></description>

</h2>
<p>These terms are often used interchangeably, but they describe different value propositions.</p>
<p>A <strong>subscription</strong> is a payment for access to content. The subscriber pays to read, watch, or listen to material that non-subscribers cannot access. The value proposition is the content itself. The New York Times, The Information, and most paywalled publications are subscription businesses. If the content stopped being published, the reason to subscribe would disappear.</p></description>

The problem is that this does not only soothe the speaker, it also instructs the listener. Wrapping a claim in the rhetoric of science or theory is not merely expressing an opinion, it asserts that the question is settled. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi belong to the Glomeromycota, an ancient fungal phylum that associates with over 80% of land plant species. They are obligate symbionts — unable to grow without a plant host — and they produce no conspicuous fruiting bodies. Their reproduction and dispersal depend on large, thick-walled spores produced in the soil. The arbuscule itself is ephemeral: individual arbuscules are produced, function for days to weeks, then collapse and are digested by the plant cell, which may then be recolonized by a new arbuscule. This cycle of formation, function, and collapse is continuous throughout the life of the mycorrhizal association.

The distinction between consonance and dissonance has been explained in acoustical terms (ratios of frequencies, coincidence of overtones), psychoacoustical terms (roughness, beating), and cultural terms (learned expectations, stylistic convention). No single explanation is sufficient. Intervals classified as dissonant in medieval European theory (the third) became the foundation of consonance in Renaissance practice. What counts as “resolved” or “at rest” is shaped by the listener’s training, tradition, and the musical context.

Like consonance, dissonance is not a fixed property of intervals but a culturally and contextually shaped perception. What sounds dissonant depends on what the listener expects, and expectations are trained by exposure to particular musical systems. The history of Western music can be read as a progressive expansion of the boundary between consonance and dissonance: intervals that sounded harsh in one century became unremarkable in the next.

The word “harmony” carries a normative connotation that is worth noting: it implies agreement, concord, things fitting together properly. This connotation has been used ideologically — to naturalize particular social arrangements as “harmonious” and to frame dissonance (musical or social) as disorder. A relational approach to harmony treats consonance and dissonance not as natural categories but as culturally constituted relations: what sounds “resolved” depends on what the listener has learned to expect.

Improvisation is inherently relational. The solo improviser relates to the instrument, to the tradition, to the room, to their own body’s state. The ensemble improviser relates to all of these and to the other musicians — listening, responding, anticipating, provoking. Call-and-response is a formalized improvisatory relation. Jazz rhythm section interaction is an informal one. Tishoumaren guitar traditions involve collective improvisation within melodic and rhythmic frameworks inherited from Tuareg musical practice.

A melody is not simply a series of notes. It is a gestalt: the listener perceives it as a whole with internal logic, not as a collection of isolated pitches. This perception depends on rhythm (the durations and accents that give the pitch sequence its shape), on contour (the pattern of ascending and descending motion), and on the melodic conventions of the listener’s musical culture. A phrase that sounds like a coherent melody in one tradition may sound like arbitrary pitches in another.

Not all music is metered. Free-rhythm performance (the alap in Hindustani classical music, recitative in opera, many forms of chant) organizes time without a recurring pulse pattern. And in many polyrhythmic traditions, the concept of a single governing meter is inadequate — the music sustains multiple metric frameworks simultaneously, and the listener’s sense of “where the beat falls” depends on which layer they attend to.

At its simplest, rhythm is a pattern of durations: long and short, stressed and unstressed, sounded and silent. But rhythm is not merely a property of the sound itself. It is a relation between the sound and the body that perceives it. A rhythm exists in the interaction between acoustic pattern and embodied expectation — the listener’s sense of where the next beat will fall, whether it arrives early, late, or not at all. This is why rhythm moves people physically: it entrains bodily processes (breathing, walking, heartbeat) into its temporal field.

In many African and Afro-diasporic musical traditions, rhythm is not a subordinate parameter serving melody but the primary organizing force. Polyrhythm — the layering of multiple independent rhythmic patterns — creates a relational field in which no single pattern is “the rhythm.” The rhythm is the interaction between patterns, and each listener or dancer may orient to a different layer. This makes rhythm a collective, perspectival phenomenon rather than a single objective structure.

Acoustically, timbre arises from the spectral content of a sound: the relative amplitudes and frequencies of the overtones that accompany the fundamental pitch, the way those overtones change over time (the “envelope”), and the noise components mixed in. But timbre is not reducible to a spectrum. It is a perceptual category — the listener’s synthesis of multiple acoustic dimensions into a single qualitative impression.

Drone-based music operates on different organizational principles from chord-progression-based music. Where tonal harmony creates movement through a sequence of changing harmonic states, a drone creates movement through the changing relationship between the moving voices and the fixed ground. The drone does not progress; the listener’s perception of it shifts as the melodic and rhythmic activity above it changes. This makes drone music fundamentally relational: the musical interest lies not in the drone or the melody alone but in the interaction between them.

Polyrhythm is central to West African, Central African, and Afro-diasporic musical traditions, where it functions not as an ornamental complexity but as the fundamental principle of rhythmic organization. In these traditions, the musical texture is a composite of interlocking parts, each with its own rhythmic identity. No single part carries “the rhythm” — the rhythm is the field of relations between parts. A listener or dancer orients to whichever layer they choose, and this choice of orientation changes the perceptual shape of the whole. This is perspectival music: the same sounding produces different rhythmic experiences depending on the participant’s point of entry.

"description": "A hook is an opening that gives the reader a reason to keep reading. The term comes from journalism (where the opening is called the lede) but applies across all writing: the first sentence, paragraph, or page must earn the reader’s attention, because no one is obligated to finish what they started.
Different genres hook in different ways:
Journalism opens with the most important information — who, what, when, where, why — because readers may stop at any point and should leave with the essential facts. Essays often open with a concrete scene, a surprising fact, a question, or a provocative claim — something that creates enough curiosity or tension to pull the reader into the argument. Fiction opens with a situation that implies instability — a character who wants something, a world that’s about to change, a voice so compelling the reader wants to keep listening. The first line of a novel carries disproportionate weight because it’s the reader’s first encounter with the voice and world. Technical writing opens with context: what is this document about, who is it for, and why should they read it. The hook is relevance — “this will help you do something you need to do.” The common mistake is opening with background, definitions, or a history of the topic. These are legitimate content but poor hooks — they ask the reader to wade through context before encountering anything they care about. The stronger move is to start with the thing the reader cares about and provide context as needed.

"description": "Protocol-aided audience analysis is Karen Schriver’s method of using think-aloud protocols to study how real readers process documents — watching and listening as they read, noting where they hesitate, misread, backtrack, or give up [@schriver1997].
Schriver distinguished three approaches to audience analysis:
Classification-based — assigning demographic categories (age, education, job role). This is the easiest and least useful: knowing that readers are “college-educated adults” doesn’t reveal what they’ll misunderstand. Intuition-based — the writer imagines a reader and predicts their responses. This is better but unreliable: Schriver’s research showed that writers systematically overestimate how well readers understand their text. Feedback-based — observing real readers using the document. Protocol-aided audience analysis is the most rigorous form of feedback-based analysis. In a protocol-aided session, a reader thinks aloud while using a document to accomplish a task. The writer (or researcher) observes without helping, recording where comprehension breaks down. The resulting data reveals problems that classification and intuition can’t detect: a heading that misleads, a paragraph that readers skip, a term that readers misinterpret.

"description": "A euphemism is a mild or indirect expression substituted for one considered too harsh, blunt, or direct. “Passed away” for “died,” “let go” for “fired,” “collateral damage” for “civilian deaths.” Euphemism softens — which is sometimes kind and sometimes dishonest, depending on what’s being softened and why.
Euphemism serves two functions:
Social courtesy. Some euphemisms smooth social interactions. “Restroom” for “toilet,” “passed away” for “died” in condolence — these reflect genuine care for the listener’s comfort. Writers may use them when the blunt term would cause unnecessary pain without adding clarity. Concealment. Other euphemisms hide reality. “Enhanced interrogation” for “torture,” “downsizing” for “mass layoffs,” “neutralize” for “kill.” George Orwell argued that political euphemism is designed to “make lies sound truthful and murder respectable” [@orwell1946]. The euphemism works by replacing a word that triggers the reader’s moral judgment with one that doesn’t. The writer’s task is to distinguish between these functions. Euphemism that respects the reader’s feelings without obscuring reality is appropriate. Euphemism that obscures reality to prevent the reader from judging it is dishonest. The test: if the reader would respond differently to the direct term than to the euphemism, the euphemism is doing political work, not social work.

The distinction between consonance and dissonance has been explained in acoustical terms (ratios of frequencies, coincidence of overtones), psychoacoustical terms (roughness, beating), and cultural terms (learned expectations, stylistic convention). No single explanation is sufficient. Intervals classified as dissonant in medieval European theory (the third) became the foundation of consonance in Renaissance practice. What counts as “resolved” or “at rest” is shaped by the listener’s training, tradition, and the musical context.

Like consonance, dissonance is not a fixed property of intervals but a culturally and contextually shaped perception. What sounds dissonant depends on what the listener expects, and expectations are trained by exposure to particular musical systems. The history of Western music can be read as a progressive expansion of the boundary between consonance and dissonance: intervals that sounded harsh in one century became unremarkable in the next.

The word “harmony” carries a normative connotation that is worth noting: it implies agreement, concord, things fitting together properly. This connotation has been used ideologically — to naturalize particular social arrangements as “harmonious” and to frame dissonance (musical or social) as disorder. A relational approach to harmony treats consonance and dissonance not as natural categories but as culturally constituted relations: what sounds “resolved” depends on what the listener has learned to expect.

Improvisation is inherently relational. The solo improviser relates to the instrument, to the tradition, to the room, to their own body’s state. The ensemble improviser relates to all of these and to the other musicians — listening, responding, anticipating, provoking. Call-and-response is a formalized improvisatory relation. Jazz rhythm section interaction is an informal one. Tishoumaren guitar traditions involve collective improvisation within melodic and rhythmic frameworks inherited from Tuareg musical practice.

A melody is not simply a series of notes. It is a gestalt: the listener perceives it as a whole with internal logic, not as a collection of isolated pitches. This perception depends on rhythm (the durations and accents that give the pitch sequence its shape), on contour (the pattern of ascending and descending motion), and on the melodic conventions of the listener’s musical culture. A phrase that sounds like a coherent melody in one tradition may sound like arbitrary pitches in another.

Not all music is metered. Free-rhythm performance (the alap in Hindustani classical music, recitative in opera, many forms of chant) organizes time without a recurring pulse pattern. And in many polyrhythmic traditions, the concept of a single governing meter is inadequate — the music sustains multiple metric frameworks simultaneously, and the listener’s sense of “where the beat falls” depends on which layer they attend to.

At its simplest, rhythm is a pattern of durations: long and short, stressed and unstressed, sounded and silent. But rhythm is not merely a property of the sound itself. It is a relation between the sound and the body that perceives it. A rhythm exists in the interaction between acoustic pattern and embodied expectation — the listener’s sense of where the next beat will fall, whether it arrives early, late, or not at all. This is why rhythm moves people physically: it entrains bodily processes (breathing, walking, heartbeat) into its temporal field.

In many African and Afro-diasporic musical traditions, rhythm is not a subordinate parameter serving melody but the primary organizing force. Polyrhythm — the layering of multiple independent rhythmic patterns — creates a relational field in which no single pattern is “the rhythm.” The rhythm is the interaction between patterns, and each listener or dancer may orient to a different layer. This makes rhythm a collective, perspectival phenomenon rather than a single objective structure.

Acoustically, timbre arises from the spectral content of a sound: the relative amplitudes and frequencies of the overtones that accompany the fundamental pitch, the way those overtones change over time (the “envelope”), and the noise components mixed in. But timbre is not reducible to a spectrum. It is a perceptual category — the listener’s synthesis of multiple acoustic dimensions into a single qualitative impression.

Drone-based music operates on different organizational principles from chord-progression-based music. Where tonal harmony creates movement through a sequence of changing harmonic states, a drone creates movement through the changing relationship between the moving voices and the fixed ground. The drone does not progress; the listener’s perception of it shifts as the melodic and rhythmic activity above it changes. This makes drone music fundamentally relational: the musical interest lies not in the drone or the melody alone but in the interaction between them.

Polyrhythm is central to West African, Central African, and Afro-diasporic musical traditions, where it functions not as an ornamental complexity but as the fundamental principle of rhythmic organization. In these traditions, the musical texture is a composite of interlocking parts, each with its own rhythmic identity. No single part carries “the rhythm” — the rhythm is the field of relations between parts. A listener or dancer orients to whichever layer they choose, and this choice of orientation changes the perceptual shape of the whole. This is perspectival music: the same sounding produces different rhythmic experiences depending on the participant’s point of entry.

This receptive quality is what makes engrossment vulnerable to failure in specific ways. The carer who substitutes their own interpretation of needs for what the cared-for actually presents has lost engrossment even if they remain emotionally engaged. A parent who “knows” what their child needs without listening has substituted projection for reception. A social worker who applies a standardized assessment without attending to the person before them has replaced engrossment with procedure. The ethical danger arises not from too much engrossment but from its absence — from caring that is technically competent but relationally empty.

"description": "A hook is an opening that gives the reader a reason to keep reading. The term comes from journalism (where the opening is called the lede) but applies across all writing: the first sentence, paragraph, or page must earn the reader’s attention, because no one is obligated to finish what they started.
Different genres hook in different ways:
Journalism opens with the most important information — who, what, when, where, why — because readers may stop at any point and should leave with the essential facts. Essays often open with a concrete scene, a surprising fact, a question, or a provocative claim — something that creates enough curiosity or tension to pull the reader into the argument. Fiction opens with a situation that implies instability — a character who wants something, a world that’s about to change, a voice so compelling the reader wants to keep listening. The first line of a novel carries disproportionate weight because it’s the reader’s first encounter with the voice and world. Technical writing opens with context: what is this document about, who is it for, and why should they read it. The hook is relevance — “this will help you do something you need to do.” The common mistake is opening with background, definitions, or a history of the topic. These are legitimate content but poor hooks — they ask the reader to wade through context before encountering anything they care about. The stronger move is to start with the thing the reader cares about and provide context as needed.

"description": "Protocol-aided audience analysis is Karen Schriver’s method of using think-aloud protocols to study how real readers process documents — watching and listening as they read, noting where they hesitate, misread, backtrack, or give up [@schriver1997].
Schriver distinguished three approaches to audience analysis:
Classification-based — assigning demographic categories (age, education, job role). This is the easiest and least useful: knowing that readers are “college-educated adults” doesn’t reveal what they’ll misunderstand. Intuition-based — the writer imagines a reader and predicts their responses. This is better but unreliable: Schriver’s research showed that writers systematically overestimate how well readers understand their text. Feedback-based — observing real readers using the document. Protocol-aided audience analysis is the most rigorous form of feedback-based analysis. In a protocol-aided session, a reader thinks aloud while using a document to accomplish a task. The writer (or researcher) observes without helping, recording where comprehension breaks down. The resulting data reveals problems that classification and intuition can’t detect: a heading that misleads, a paragraph that readers skip, a term that readers misinterpret.

"description": "A euphemism is a mild or indirect expression substituted for one considered too harsh, blunt, or direct. “Passed away” for “died,” “let go” for “fired,” “collateral damage” for “civilian deaths.” Euphemism softens — which is sometimes kind and sometimes dishonest, depending on what’s being softened and why.
Euphemism serves two functions:
Social courtesy. Some euphemisms smooth social interactions. “Restroom” for “toilet,” “passed away” for “died” in condolence — these reflect genuine care for the listener’s comfort. Writers may use them when the blunt term would cause unnecessary pain without adding clarity. Concealment. Other euphemisms hide reality. “Enhanced interrogation” for “torture,” “downsizing” for “mass layoffs,” “neutralize” for “kill.” George Orwell argued that political euphemism is designed to “make lies sound truthful and murder respectable” [@orwell1946]. The euphemism works by replacing a word that triggers the reader’s moral judgment with one that doesn’t. The writer’s task is to distinguish between these functions. Euphemism that respects the reader’s feelings without obscuring reality is appropriate. Euphemism that obscures reality to prevent the reader from judging it is dishonest. The test: if the reader would respond differently to the direct term than to the euphemism, the euphemism is doing political work, not social work.

The problem is that this does not only soothe the speaker, it also instructs the listener. Wrapping a claim in the rhetoric of science or theory is not merely expressing an opinion, it asserts that the question is settled. Because academic fluency and leisure are unevenly distributed, many people cannot realistically verify these claims without substantial unpaid effort. Authority ends up doing the work that evidence should be doing.

What is offensive about this is not the presence of fear. Fear is understandable in the face of genuinely difficult systems. What is offensive is the use of elite rhetorical tools to offload that fear onto an audience as certainty. This is pedagogy as displacement, where incomplete understanding is transformed into final-sounding explanation. The response was not better single predictions, but a different way of listening. Meteorology moved toward ensemble forecasting: running many simulations, each plausible, none authoritative. The question shifted from “what will the weather be?” to “what kinds of weather are now possible?” This was not a retreat from rigor. It was an admission that in a non-stationary system, insisting on a single correct performance is a category error. The musician stops trying to play the piece right and starts trying to stay oriented within a field of possible sounds.

What adapting without stationarity and ergodicity looks like is not Bach played faster. It looks more like jazz, or like communal musics that never relied on a fixed score to begin with. In jazz, there is structure, but it lives in shared constraints rather than scripted outcomes: key centers that can bend, rhythms that can fracture and reassemble, motifs that are offered, taken up, distorted, or dropped entirely. Skill matters—but it is skill at listening, at responding, at leaving space. Mastery is not the ability to reproduce a piece, but to remain musically coherent when the piece dissolves.

The danger is not that people will fail to adapt. The danger is that they will insist on adapting as if the music were still the same, and mistake fidelity for preparedness. Implication only works when the key holds. In a world where the score is dissolving in real time, adaptation becomes less about getting the right notes and more about sustaining the capacity to listen, respond, and remain in relation. Not playing Bach better, but learning how to make music together when there is no longer a piece to return to.

description: Annual vine cultivar of Ipomoea purpurea, 60-75 days to first flower. Vigorous twining vine 2-3.5 m. Blue, purple, pink, or bicolored ephemeral flowers open at dawn, close by mid-morning. Full sun, moderate soil. Poor soil yields more flowers (nitrogen limitation). Prolific seeder; allow plants to complete seed maturation for self-sowing next season or deadhead to extend flowering.

Morning glory cultivation grows [Ipomoea purpurea](../../../../../../../science/theories/biology/theories/botany/terms/ipomoea-purpurea.md) as a vigorous annual vine with prolific blue, purple, pink, or bicolored flowers that open each morning and close by noon. The ephemeral daily flowering pattern is distinctive; sustained bloom from mid-summer through first frost makes morning glories reliable cover for trellises, fences, and pergolas.

Ramp flavor is mild garlic-onion with tender, succulent leaves available only in spring (March-May in the northern US). For more sophisticated NPC behavior, Discworld implements an event system: NPCs can subscribe to event classes (`event_listen_say()`, `event_person_tell()`). When a say happens in a room, the NPC's event handler is called with the speaker and text. The NPC can then decide whether to respond, start combat, or ignore the message.

This implements **M4** (every message names its receivers) with asymmetry: a player's say is broadcast to all objects in the room, but which objects *care* is determined by their subscriptions. NPCs are not forced to hear everything — they can filter by listener pattern (e.g., a shopkeeper hears only customers, a guard hears only unauthorized intruders).

This is a settlement path in the substrate's sense. An I/O operation initially settled at the most expensive layer (inference reads and summarizes) is *the same operation* as one settled at the cheapest layer (interfacer composes). The migration from one to the other is the substrate gaining content: more predications on relevant entities, more vocabulary in the relevant scope, more declared rules that determine the answer from structural composition rather than from inference. Every operation that descends the path is a permanent cost reduction, because the structural facts the substrate now uses to answer the question are themselves substrate content — auditable, replicable, and inspectable — rather than ephemeral inference at call time.

- **Persistence-binding compatible.** The persistence-binding must match the target's persistence model. A deployment to an ephemeral target without persistent-volume binding is admissible only for transient workloads.

- **Branches without 0-cell identity.** A "branch" that has no substrate-recorded settling — pure runtime state — is not a 0-cell of the groupoid. The substrate refuses such ephemeral branches; per [self-representation](../concepts/self-representation.md), branches are substrate content.

**Part 4: Transport switching mid-federation.** When a federation switches transports (e.g., a TCP connection drops and reconnects via WebSocket), in-flight messages from the dropped connection are retransmitted on the new connection. Per [federation-convergence](federation-convergence.md)'s order-independence, retransmissions are safe — duplicates are deduplicated by hash, missed-original-deliveries are recovered by the retransmission. The converged state is unaffected.

- **Transport upgrades without downtime.** Switching from one transport to another (HTTP → WebSocket for lower latency, TCP → TLS-TCP for added security) does not require federation-state migration. The substrate continues federation seamlessly across the transport change.

The [hidden curriculum](./hidden-curriculum.md) is the set of lessons that educational institutions teach without explicitly intending to — through their structures, routines, social relations, and unstated assumptions rather than through their formal content. Students learn not only what is taught but also what is practiced: how time is organized, who speaks and who listens, what questions are permitted, what counts as success, and whose knowledge is valued.

[Paulo Freire](../../../../../../../references/people/paulo-freire.md), in *Pedagogy of the Oppressed* (1968/1970), described conventional education as the **[banking model](../terms/banking-model.md)**: the teacher deposits knowledge into passive students, who receive, memorize, and repeat it. The teacher knows; the student does not. The teacher speaks; the student listens. Knowledge flows in one direction.

- **[Land as pedagogy](../terms/land-based-education.md).** The land is not a backdrop for learning; it is the teacher. Knowledge comes from sustained, attentive relationship with place — observing, participating, listening. This is not metaphorical: specific knowledge (ecological, medicinal, ceremonial, political) is held in specific places and transmitted through practices of being in those places.

Drone-based music operates on different organizational principles from chord-progression-based music. Where [tonal](../theories/music-theory/terms/tonality.md) [harmony](../theories/music-theory/terms/harmony.md) creates movement through a sequence of changing harmonic states, a drone creates movement through the changing *relationship* between the moving voices and the fixed ground. The drone does not progress; the listener's perception of it shifts as the melodic and rhythmic activity above it changes. This makes drone music fundamentally relational: the musical interest lies not in the drone or the melody alone but in the interaction between them.

Polyrhythm is central to West African, Central African, and Afro-diasporic musical traditions, where it functions not as an ornamental complexity but as the fundamental principle of rhythmic organization. In these traditions, the musical texture is a composite of interlocking parts, each with its own rhythmic identity. No single part carries "the rhythm" — the rhythm is the field of relations between parts. A listener or dancer orients to whichever layer they choose, and this choice of orientation changes the perceptual shape of the whole. This is perspectival music: the same sounding produces different rhythmic experiences depending on the participant's point of entry.

In contrast to this asymmetry, many Indigenous and relational traditions treat emotion not as the interior property of a sovereign self, but as a **co-emergent field phenomenon**—something that arises _in the between_, through proximity, movement, silence, and listening. As **Leanne Betasamosake Simpson** and others have argued, relation is not built through confession or explanation, but through **reciprocal attunement**—learning to sense when another is withdrawing, overextending, contracting, or offering. In such a field, emotion is not the justification for retreat or re-centering, but a signal to shift rhythm, deepen listening, or pause without fleeing.

To feel harm across difference requires the **suspension of the demand for symmetry**. In this practice, the settler subject must resist the impulse to reconfigure the event in a way that preserves their own moral coherence. Instead, they must let the harm **stand**—in its language, its logic, its affective weight. This does not mean agreeing with every account, but recognizing that **explanation is not owed**, and that emotional discomfort is not a signal to clarify, but a **cue to listen differently**.

Crucially, this is not passive listening. It is an **active affective labor** of _holding open space_ for something that will not resolve on the settler’s terms. This kind of presence is not trained by liberal selfhood—it must be **cultivated through practice**, often in tension with the dominant subject’s instincts and acculturation toward comfort, clarity, and closure.

As an imperial language, Latin functioned through a layered system of **semiotic stratification**. At one level, it offered vocabulary for governance: law, contract, property, command. At another, it structured the rules of morphology, syntax, and elocution through which **subject-positions** could be articulated at all. Unlike many vernaculars, Latin positioned its core grammatical operations—tense, number, mood, case—within a complex system of **inflectional suffixes** located in **prosodically weak positions**: word endings. These suffixes, often unstressed, were where the full epistemic and legal status of a noun or verb was encoded. Thus, Latin trained its speakers to _listen for meaning in the faintest parts of a word_—an acoustical pedagogy of discipline. In such a field, emotion is not the justification for retreat or re-centering, but a signal to shift rhythm, deepen listening, or pause without fleeing.

To feel harm across difference requires the **suspension of the demand for symmetry**. In this practice, the settler subject must resist the impulse to reconfigure the event in a way that preserves their own moral coherence. Instead, they must let the harm **stand**—in its language, its logic, its affective weight. This does not mean agreeing with every account, but recognizing that **explanation is not owed**, and that emotional discomfort is not a signal to clarify, but a **cue to listen differently**.

Crucially, this is not passive listening. It is an **active affective labor** of _holding open space_ for something that will not resolve on the settler’s terms. This kind of presence is not trained by liberal selfhood—it must be **cultivated through practice**, often in tension with the dominant subject’s instincts and acculturation toward comfort, clarity, and closure.

As an imperial language, Latin functioned through a layered system of **semiotic stratification**. At one level, it offered vocabulary for governance: law, contract, property, command. At another, it structured the rules of morphology, syntax, and elocution through which **subject-positions** could be articulated at all. Unlike many vernaculars, Latin positioned its core grammatical operations—tense, number, mood, case—within a complex system of **inflectional suffixes** located in **prosodically weak positions**: word endings. These suffixes, often unstressed, were where the full epistemic and legal status of a noun or verb was encoded. Thus, Latin trained its speakers to _listen for meaning in the faintest parts of a word_—an acoustical pedagogy of discipline. The ears and mouths of colonial subjects had to be reshaped to perform and perceive Roman authority not only as content but as **phonological form**.

Invocation in this context is not a mere mental or verbal act—it is **embodied, sounded, and spatial**. The rain stick’s slow cascade of sound mimics the quality of rain not to trick nature, but to **attune the human field to the possibility of relation**. It invites rain not by demanding it, but by **performing the condition of receptivity**. The sound marks a space of listening and humility. In many desert rituals, this would be accompanied by coca offerings, drumming, or song—further enactments of _ayni_, the Andean principle of reciprocity.

Such an ecology of knowledge is not closed or esoteric. It is transmitted through practice, memory, and care—through the slow crafting of a cactus tube, the listening to its fall, the feel of seeds over spines. The rain stick teaches that in worlds where every element is alive with relation, even sound itself can become a form of listening.

As an imperial language, Latin functioned through a layered system of **semiotic stratification**. At one level, it offered vocabulary for governance: law, contract, property, command. At another, it structured the rules of morphology, syntax, and elocution through which **subject-positions** could be articulated at all. Unlike many vernaculars, Latin positioned its core grammatical operations—tense, number, mood, case—within a complex system of **inflectional suffixes** located in **prosodically weak positions**: word endings. These suffixes, often unstressed, were where the full epistemic and legal status of a noun or verb was encoded. Thus, Latin trained its speakers to _listen for meaning in the faintest parts of a word_—an acoustical pedagogy of discipline. The ears and mouths of colonial subjects had to be reshaped to perform and perceive Roman authority not only as content but as **phonological form**.

Invocation in this context is not a mere mental or verbal act—it is **embodied, sounded, and spatial**. The rain stick’s slow cascade of sound mimics the quality of rain not to trick nature, but to **attune the human field to the possibility of relation**. It invites rain not by demanding it, but by **performing the condition of receptivity**. The sound marks a space of listening and humility. In many desert rituals, this would be accompanied by coca offerings, drumming, or song—further enactments of _ayni_, the Andean principle of reciprocity.

Such an ecology of knowledge is not closed or esoteric. It is transmitted through practice, memory, and care—through the slow crafting of a cactus tube, the listening to its fall, the feel of seeds over spines. The rain stick teaches that in worlds where every element is alive with relation, even sound itself can become a form of listening.

abstract = {Brain oscillations are prevalent in all species and are involved in numerous perceptual operations. α oscillations are thought to facilitate processing through the inhibition of task-irrelevant networks, while β oscillations are linked to the putative reactivation of content representations. Can the proposed functional role of α and β oscillations be generalized from low-level operations to higher-level cognitive processes? Here we address this question focusing on naturalistic spoken language comprehension. Twenty-two (18 female) Dutch native speakers listened to stories in Dutch and French while MEG was recorded. We used dependency parsing to identify three dependency states at each word: the number of (1) newly opened dependencies, (2) dependencies that remained open, and (3) resolved dependencies. We then constructed forward models to predict α and β power from the dependency features. Results showed that dependency features predict α and β power in language-related regions beyond low-level linguistic features. Left temporal, fundamental language regions are involved in language comprehension in α, while frontal and parietal, higher-order language regions, and motor regions are involved in β. Critically, α- and β-band dynamics seem to subserve language comprehension tapping into syntactic structure building and semantic composition by providing low-level mechanistic operations for inhibition and reactivation processes. Because of the temporal similarity of the α-β responses, their potential functional dissociation remains to be elucidated. Overall, this study sheds light on the role of α and β oscillations during naturalistic spoken language comprehension, providing evidence for the generalizability of these dynamics from perceptual to complex linguistic processes.

SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT It remains unclear whether the proposed functional role of α and β oscillations in perceptual and motor function is generalizable to higher-level cognitive processes, such as spoken language comprehension. We found that syntactic features predict α and β power in language-related regions beyond low-level linguistic features when listening to naturalistic speech in a known language. We offer experimental findings that integrate a neuroscientific framework on the role of brain oscillations as “building blocks” with spoken language comprehension. This supports the view of a domain-general role of oscillations across the hierarchy of cognitive functions, from low-level sensory operations to abstract linguistic processes.},

abstract = {When listening to spoken narratives, we must integrate information over multiple, concurrent timescales, building up from words to sentences to paragraphs to a coherent narrative. Recent evidence suggests that the brain relies on a chain of hierarchically organized areas with increasing temporal receptive windows to process naturalistic narratives. We hypothesized that the structure of this cortical processing hierarchy should result in an observable sequence of response lags between networks comprising the hierarchy during narrative comprehension. This study uses functional MRI to estimate the response lags between functional networks during narrative comprehension. We use intersubject cross-correlation analysis to capture network connectivity driven by the shared stimulus. We found a fixed temporal sequence of response lags—on the scale of several seconds—starting in early auditory areas, followed by language areas, the attention network, and lastly the default mode network. This gradient is consistent across eight distinct stories but absent in data acquired during rest or using a scrambled story stimulus, supporting our hypothesis that narrative construction gives rise to internetwork lags. Finally, we build a simple computational model for the neural dynamics underlying the construction of nested narrative features. Our simulations illustrate how the gradual accumulation of information within the boundaries of nested linguistic events, accompanied by increased activity at each level of the processing hierarchy, can give rise to the observed lag gradient.},
