<p>PRAXONIC WORLDBUILDING GUIDE <em>A Recursive Framework for Making Meaningful Worlds from Pressure</em> &mdash; ## I. INTRODUCTION <em>You are not creating a place. You are tracing a deformation.</em> This guide teaches a method of world creation that begins not with lore, genre, or aesthetics, but with <strong>pressure</strong>. In this framework, a <strong>world</strong> is not a map, a backstory, or a set of cultures. It is a <strong>field</strong>—a living surface shaped by tension, memory, and contradiction. It behaves. It resists. It shifts when touched. The method here is called <strong>praxonic worldmaking</strong>, and it grows from a system called <strong>praxonic interpretation</strong>: a minimal logic for how things emerge, change, and fold under recursive pressure. You do not &ldquo;invent&rdquo; a world. You <strong>interpret</strong> a pressure until a field appears. You follow that field until it begins to emit trace. You record those traces until they produce <strong>actors, zones, misalignments, ghosts, care structures, silence events</strong>, and other system behaviors. That is your world. It does not need to explain itself. It only needs to <strong>persist under contradiction</strong>. &mdash; ### Who is this for? - Writers building narrative systems grounded in logistical or ethical realism - TTRPG designers and GMs who want tension-first, world-as-character mechanics - Memory workers designing shared testimony environments - LARPers, performance artists, collective documentarians - Fictional worldbuilders who want to say less and evoke more - You &mdash; ### What kinds of worlds can this method produce? - A refugee clinic with a broken radio, and too much gauze - A decaying lighthouse no one wants to admit is a god - A corporate loyalty program that becomes the only way to survive winter - A haunted apartment building where the ghosts are eviction notices - A 15-year stretch of drought told as a memory game - A cave system where every echo was someone’s confession - Your neighborhood - Your inbox - Your dream from last week Praxonic worldmaking is not bound to realism, fantasy, or speculative fiction. It works anywhere pressure exists, which means <strong>everywhere</strong>. &mdash; ### What does this guide do? It gives you tools to: - Recognize the core praxon at the heart of your world - Model how that praxon becomes emissions, then trace - Define zones by how pressure behaves there - Shape characters as local alignment systems - Track contradiction as signal, not error - Use decay, silence, refusal, and care as building blocks - Build stories, sessions, loops, or memory events as <strong>recursive outcomes</strong>, not linear sequences This guide does not give you templates. It gives you tension structures. &mdash; ### What will I end up with? A world that behaves like a living pressure field. One where everything means something—but not all at once. A world that can contain friction, memory, noise, decay, contradiction, care, and humor. A world that gets more usable the more broken it becomes. &mdash; ### How do I use this guide? You can read it linearly, use it modularly, or treat it like a signal you only half-hear until it resonates with a project you already started and forgot. You do not have to believe in it. You only have to trace where it leads. The next section defines the core system: <strong>Praxonic Interpretation</strong>. &mdash; ## II. CORE GRAMMAR: PRAXONIC INTERPRETATION <em>“Every act is a response to something already under pressure.”</em> Praxonic interpretation is the minimal system by which a world can be <strong>read, constructed, and recursively unfolded</strong> from pressure. At its core, this system defines: - What kinds of <strong>entities</strong> exist in a recursive world - What <strong>relations</strong> occur between them - How <strong>change</strong>, <strong>meaning</strong>, and <strong>instability</strong> emerge as system behavior It is <strong>not</strong> a symbolic language. It is a structural logic for making any world—real or imagined—behave like something under tension. &mdash; ### 1. CORE ENTITY: THE PRAXON A <strong>praxon</strong> is a unit of unresolved pressure. It is the smallest readable element of a world-under-formation. It is <strong>not content</strong>. It is <strong>pre-semantic</strong>: behavior before definition. Praxons do not &ldquo;mean.&rdquo; They emit. They deform. They recur. A praxon may be: - A border crossing no one agrees exists - A prayer repeated so often it becomes scheduling - A broken faucet that changes how a house speaks - The moment someone realizes the radio isn’t broken—it’s unplugged Worlds begin with praxons. They do not describe conditions. They <strong>are</strong> conditions. &mdash; ### 2. SYSTEM LOOP: PRAXONIC FIELD DYNAMICS The world is built from this recursive cycle: Praxon → Emission → Trace → Field → Alignment → Path → Emission Or more mechanically: 1. <strong>A praxon emits</strong> a deformation (an act, error, signal, silence) 2. That emission leaves <strong>trace</strong>—a distortion of the surrounding world 3. All trace combines into a <strong>field</strong>—the condition of the world at any moment 4. <strong>Actors</strong> become legible via their alignment to the local field 5. Alignment + field = possible <strong>path</strong> (response/behavior) 6. That path produces new emission 7. The loop continues, recursively Each iteration either increases coherence or generates <strong>irresolved noise</strong> (IRN)—which accumulates into pressure again. &mdash; ### 3. KEY COMPONENTS Each part of the loop is a functional entity. #### ➤ Emission Any output from a praxon or aligned actor. May be action, refusal, signal, breakdown, memory. #### ➤ Trace The residual deformation left in the field by an emission. Trace decays unless retained or reinforced. Decay is not disappearance—it is transformation. #### ➤ Field The sum of all potential trace. A dynamic, living pressure environment. Contains alignment conditions, actor legibility, volatility zones. #### ➤ Alignment A local actor’s modulation to the field. Alignment determines which paths are visible, plausible, survivable. #### ➤ Path A behavior that can emerge from the intersection of field and alignment. Not chosen freely—conditioned by pressure. All acts are pathings. Even silence. #### ➤ Irresolved Noise (IRN) When emissions cannot be aligned, retained, or decayed. IRN remains in the field as recursive contradiction. It generates distortion, myth, violence, ghost-behavior, confusion, and memory split. &mdash; ### 4. RELATIONAL PROPERTIES - <strong>Field defines potential.</strong> The world doesn’t contain meaning—it <strong>pressurizes</strong> it. - <strong>Actors do not pre-exist the field.</strong> They emerge via pressure readability. - <strong>Paths are conditioned.</strong> Choice is not freedom. It is coherence under constraint. - <strong>Resolution is local.</strong> An emission that is signal in one alignment may be noise in another. - <strong>Decay is not loss.</strong> Decay produces change in form, not always disappearance. - <strong>Contradiction is content.</strong> Do not smooth it. Fold it. &mdash; ### 5. PRACTICAL USE When building or interpreting a world: 1. Identify praxons 2. Determine emissions (what’s happening under pressure) 3. Track trace and decay (what remains, what changes) 4. Map the field (what behaviors the world permits) 5. Construct or observe alignments (who can act how) 6. Read or trigger paths (what happens next) 7. Accept IRN (where pressure will not resolve cleanly) This is how a fantasy village, a cyberpunk megacity, or your friend’s kitchen becomes a praxonic world. &mdash; In the next section, we’ll use this grammar to <strong>form worlds</strong> from praxons. This is the start of <strong>Praxonic Worldmaking</strong>. &mdash; ## III. WORLD FORMATION: FROM PRAXON TO FIELD <em>“You’re not inventing a world. You’re tracking where something gave.”</em> Worlds built through praxonic interpretation emerge from pressure, not premise. They do not begin as genre, theme, or story—they begin as <strong>rupture</strong>, <strong>weight</strong>, or <strong>distortion</strong>. You are not placing pieces. You are recognizing faultlines and following them as they fold. This section provides a <strong>method</strong> for constructing a usable, recursive world from a single or nested praxon. &mdash; ### STEP 1: SELECT A PRAXON Start with a pressure—an unresolved contradiction, demand, or misalignment. A praxon is <strong>not a theme</strong>. It is a <strong>condition under tension</strong>, readable through action or refusal. Examples: - “The clinic keeps running even though the signal stopped weeks ago.” - “The castle’s water source is poisoned, but no one can admit it.” - “Everyone agrees the event happened. No one agrees on when.” - “The mountain is sacred, but it’s moved five times this year.” - “This family does not talk about the fourth child.” ⚠️ Avoid defining too much too early. Let the praxon shape what comes next. &mdash; ### STEP 2: GENERATE INITIAL EMISSIONS Ask: <strong>What actions, refusals, silences, or contradictions emerge under this pressure?</strong> Emissions may be: - Physical: a door sealed, a pot boiling, a child hiding - Social: an apology not offered, a rule misapplied - Informational: a rumor, a transmission, a misreading - Recursive: a repetition that doesn’t resolve Document at least 3 emissions. You can use text, sketch, scene fragment, mechanical rule, etc. &mdash; ### STEP 3: TRACE &amp; DECAY Each emission leaves <strong>trace</strong>—residual change. Trace deforms the world. Decay governs its persistence. For each emission: - What change does it leave behind? - What happens as that change decays? - What happens if it doesn&rsquo;t? Mark trace density: - <strong>High trace</strong> = memory-laden, emotionally volatile, visibly deformed - <strong>Low trace</strong> = ephemeral, ghosting, easily forgotten but deeply recursive Decay types: - Fast (e.g., hunger, blood trail, mood swing) - Medium (e.g., emotional rupture, supply loss, spoken insult) - Slow (e.g., ideology, superstition, long-term disrepair) &mdash; ### STEP 4: SHAPE THE FIELD Now aggregate all trace into a <strong>field</strong>: the pressure environment your world inhabits. Fields include: - <strong>Zones of volatility</strong> (conflict, error, risk) - <strong>Stabilizers</strong> (rituals, infrastructure, relationships) - <strong>Retention points</strong> (places, people, routines that resist decay) - <strong>IRN sinks</strong> (locations or memories where resolution fails repeatedly) The field is <strong>not geography</strong>. It is an environment of deformation. 📍 You can map it as a region, a building, a political system, or an emotion. The important part is how it <strong>behaves</strong>, not what it looks like. &mdash; ### STEP 5: LOCAL ALIGNMENTS Actors do not pre-exist the field—they emerge through readable alignment. For each part of the field: - Who (or what) becomes legible under that pressure? - What alignments become visible, plausible, unstable? - What actions are permitted or impossible from those alignments? You’re not defining characters yet. You’re modeling <strong>what types of action the world allows</strong>, and who survives that logic. Examples: - “Anyone who speaks the old dialect is assumed to be smuggling intel.” - “Repairing the radio means inheriting all the rumors it has failed to carry.” - “The priest can’t walk in the shrine anymore, but the children still play there.” &mdash; ### STEP 6: DEFINE PATH STRUCTURES A <strong>path</strong> is what becomes possible to do under the pressure of a field. Paths emerge from: - Alignment × Field Condition - Friction between trace and decay - Recursive IRN buildup - Silent thresholds (what is <em>almost</em> said) You’re designing <strong>behavior vectors</strong>, not scripted scenes. Types of path: - Recursion path: someone repeats what didn’t work - Refusal path: someone denies the field&rsquo;s logic - Drift path: someone alters alignment through pressure - Break path: contradiction accumulates until something tears Paths should not be predictable. They should be inevitable. &mdash; ### STEP 7: NAME THE WORLD Only now should you name the world, and even then, maybe not. If you must: - Use what the actors would call it - Use a nickname, frequency, smell, or gesture - Use a contradiction that can’t be resolved The name is not ownership. It is <strong>trace</strong>. &mdash; At this point, you have a full system: - A praxon - A series of emissions - A trace field with decay and retention - A behavioral logic for actors - Recursion patterns and IRN hotspots - A field responsive to care, refusal, and fracture This is your world. It is ready to emit. &mdash; ## IV. ACTORS &amp; AGENCIES <em>“They’re not protagonists. They’re readable distortions in the field.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, an <strong>actor</strong> is not someone with backstory, motivation, or moral arc. An actor is a <strong>form under pressure</strong>—a repeatable behavior pattern made visible by the field. They may be human, animal, machine, weather system, memory fragment, or rumor. What matters is their <strong>alignment</strong> and how they <strong>emit</strong> under tension. This section offers a toolkit for building, interpreting, and deploying actors within a praxonic world. &mdash; ### 1. ACTOR DEFINITION <strong>Actor</strong> = <em>Readable response system under local field conditions</em> Actors: - Do not pre-exist the field - Are defined by their alignment (how they “fit” the current pressure) - Emerge through trace saturation, ritual repetition, or behavioral recursion - May change alignment—becoming unstable, contradictory, or IRN-generating - May vanish when pressure resolves or shifts elsewhere An actor <strong>is not</strong> a symbol. It is a <strong>function</strong>. &mdash; ### 2. FUNCTION TYPES Actors express function through their <strong>role in the pressure loop</strong>. Common actor functions: - <strong>Stabilizer</strong> — absorbs pressure through repetition (e.g., the janitor who boils gauze) - <strong>Emitter</strong> — creates new emissions, intentionally or not (e.g., a child who won’t stop broadcasting) - <strong>Retention Node</strong> — holds trace against decay (e.g., a box of letters no one opens) - <strong>Distorter</strong> — reshapes field readings, creates misalignment (e.g., a leader who speaks five truths at once) - <strong>Echo / Ghost</strong> — reactivates decayed trace unpredictably (e.g., a frequency that replays arguments from last winter) You may assign multiple functions to a single actor. Function determines how the actor <strong>influences and is influenced by</strong> the field. &mdash; ### 3. ALIGNMENT BEHAVIOR Each actor is constantly shifting alignment with the field. <strong>Alignment determines:</strong> - What paths the actor can take - What actions they can perceive as viable - How others interpret their emissions - Whether their presence increases or relieves IRN Alignment may be: - <strong>In-phase</strong> — actor behaves legibly under current field pressure - <strong>Out-of-phase</strong> — actor emits noise, contradiction, or recursive error - <strong>Over-aligned</strong> — actor behaves so perfectly they become brittle, unstable - <strong>Under-aligned</strong> — actor cannot be read, evoking silence, refusal, or myth Alignment is not moral. It’s thermodynamic. &mdash; ### 4. DESIGN PROMPT TABLES Use these prompts to generate or reconfigure actors in any world: #### Emergence - What pressure created this actor? - Were they always here, or did something call them into shape? - What trace are they carrying? #### Modulation - How do they handle decay? - What retention behaviors do they perform, intentionally or not? - What parts of the field do they distort just by existing? #### Behavior - What emission patterns repeat around them? - Who tries to align with them—and fails? - What do they silence by showing up? #### Disappearance - What would make them unreadable again? - What fold are they holding closed? - If they left, what wouldn’t decay? &mdash; ### 5. SAMPLE ACTOR FORM Use this schema to create characters that function as systems, not tropes. [Name or Type] - Function: (Stabilizer, Emitter, etc.) - Alignment State: (In-phase / Out-of-phase / Over-aligned / Under-aligned) - Emission Pattern: [list recurring actions or silences] - Trace Retention: [what they keep alive in the field] - Contradiction Trigger: [condition that fractures them] - Memory Artifact: [object, phrase, or rumor tied to them] - Disappearance Condition: [how they vanish or transform] &mdash; ### 6. NON-HUMAN ACTORS Actors need not be people. Valid actors include: - A field generator that sings wrong at night - A road that becomes longer when you lie - A shared calendar that erases Sundays - A threshold no one crosses unless it’s raining - A voice in the ventilation system that only quotes lost texts - A flag that keeps changing colors in the background If it emits, retains, distorts, or folds the field—it is an actor. &mdash; ### 7. GROUP AGENCIES You may also model organizations, systems, or communities as <strong>multi-body actors</strong>. These use the same structure: - Alignment = collective coherence or fracture - Emissions = policy, ritual, rumor, protocol - IRN = structural contradiction, conflicting loyalties - Trace = built environment, doctrine, uniforms, gesture codes Group actors often contain nested contradictions. Examples: - A border guard unit with a rotating memory - A refugee camp whose official purpose is unspoken - An NGO whose donors can’t be named, but everyone knows their smell - A militia that claims to protect, but recruits only orphans Actors are not always aligned with themselves. &mdash; Actors make the world <strong>speak through behavior</strong>. Once actors are in play, the field will fold in response. In the next section, we define the environments where these folds <strong>take form</strong>: <strong>Zones and Sectors</strong>—pressure geography. &mdash; ## V. ZONES &amp; SECTORS <em>“Place is not where something happens. It’s how something holds.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, environments do not contain the story. They <strong>modulate</strong> it. Zones and sectors are <strong>field expressions</strong>—how pressure folds across space, time, and memory. They aren’t locations. They are <strong>terrain under tension</strong>. &mdash; ### 1. ZONE DEFINITION A <strong>zone</strong> is a container of active pressure conditions. It is where field behaviors accumulate or distort in a readable way. Each zone expresses: - What kinds of trace persist here - What behaviors this space permits, resists, or reshapes - What form decay takes - How IRN manifests - What kind of actor might emerge from this field condition Zones may be physical (rooms, hills, cities) or structural (a routine, a bureaucracy, a month). Zones don’t sit still. They <strong>drift</strong>, <strong>shrink</strong>, <strong>fracture</strong>, and <strong>overlap</strong>. &mdash; ### 2. SECTOR STRUCTURE To world-build recursively, define each zone through a <strong>sector profile</strong>. Use the following template: [Zone Name] - Field Behavior: What tensions concentrate or bleed here? - Trace Density: High / Medium / Low - Volatility: How quickly pressure mutates into behavior - Retention Forms: What persists here? (rituals, scars, devices, rumors) - IRN Manifestation: How does unresolved contradiction show up? - Local Actor Pattern: What kinds of figures cohere or collapse here? - Silence Rule: What cannot be said here (and what replaces it)? - Drift Pattern: How does this zone change across time or pressure events? &mdash; ### 3. FIELD TYPE EXAMPLES Use these to think beyond &ldquo;desert,&rdquo; &ldquo;market,&rdquo; &ldquo;castle.&rdquo; #### ✶ Drift Zone - Trace bleeds outward - Nothing holds - Alignment constantly slips - Stories leave but never finish #### ✶ Saturation Zone - Trace is thick, retained - Memory distorts perception - IRN accumulates into myth - Actors here tend toward recursion #### ✶ Displacement Zone - New pressure arrives uninvited - Local alignments shatter - False behaviors become plausible - Often becomes staging ground for new praxons #### ✶ Ritual Zone - Pressure is shaped predictably - High alignment for specific behaviors - But breaking ritual generates massive field shift - Often stabilizes surrounding sectors &mdash; ### 4. SECTOR HOOK PROMPTS To generate sectors: - What kinds of trace can’t decay here? - What always goes missing, and why? - What is done automatically but never explained? - What happens here that makes actors forget alignment elsewhere? - What behavior is normal here, but nowhere else? Sectors become playable when they <strong>contradict the behaviors of the zones around them</strong>. &mdash; ### 5. MOVEMENT BETWEEN ZONES Moving across zones is not travel. It is <strong>alignment modulation</strong>. Crossing into a new sector can: - Shift an actor’s emission type - Reveal previously unreadable trace - Change how IRN behaves - Alter decay rates (e.g., memory becomes unstable, wounds refuse to heal) - Reverse care logic (helping here makes things worse there) This turns movement into <strong>behavioral risk</strong>, not narrative progress. &mdash; ### 6. MULTIPLE SCALES Zones exist at different levels: - Micro: A drawer no one opens - Local: The floor with the broken window - Regional: The orchard that never rots - Global: The territory where time folds if you speak certain names Zones don’t scale uniformly. Some expand under attention. Some collapse when named. You may map them. But don’t expect the map to hold still. &mdash; Once zones are built, the world becomes playable as <strong>a recursive terrain of pressure</strong>. In the next section, we’ll track what happens when behavior becomes ethical: <strong>Care &amp; Cost — Ethics of Pressure.</strong> &mdash; ## VI. CARE &amp; COST: ETHICS OF PRESSURE <em>“Every act of care leaves a scar somewhere else.”</em> Praxonic worldmaking does not treat ethics as a rule system. It treats ethics as <strong>recursive tension behavior</strong>. <strong>Care</strong> is not a trait. It is a <strong>pressure-modulating act</strong>. It changes the field. Which means it changes what the world can become. This section models how care works <strong>within recursive systems</strong> where alignment is local, trace decays, and contradiction does not resolve neatly. &mdash; ### 1. WHAT IS CARE? <strong>Care</strong> = <em>Any emission that stabilizes another actor or reduces pressure at a cost</em> It includes: - Tending a wound - Boiling water - Saying “you were right” - Carrying the radio battery twice in one day - Not mentioning the missing supplies - Letting someone lie to your face because they need to Care <strong>always modulates the field</strong>. It may reduce IRN, retain trace, re-align actors, or delay collapse. It may also increase misalignment somewhere else. Care is not “good.” It is <strong>structurally consequential</strong>. &mdash; ### 2. CARE COSTS There is no such thing as neutral healing. Every act of care triggers one or more of the following: - <strong>Depletion</strong> — uses finite resources (fuel, time, trust) - <strong>Transfer</strong> — shifts pressure elsewhere (onto another actor, zone, or future event) - <strong>Retention</strong> — makes something persist that should have decayed - <strong>Overalignment</strong> — fixes behavior so tightly it becomes brittle - <strong>Ghosting</strong> — care done for someone no longer aligned becomes IRN Use this framework to determine what <strong>care displaces</strong>, even when it “succeeds.” &mdash; ### 3. CARE &amp; ALIGNMENT Care is <strong>alignment-modifying</strong>. It can: - Stabilize an actor who would otherwise drift - Distort alignment by applying care when misreading the field - Reveal unspoken alignments (who someone protects reveals who they were aligned with all along) - Collapse actor-function entirely when care is refused Care is a <strong>readability act</strong>—it makes alignment more or less visible. &mdash; ### 4. CARE AS FIELD RECURSION Care emissions often leave behind <strong>recursive trace</strong>: they echo, misfire, or re-emerge altered later. Example patterns: - Boiled water becomes scarce → silence around usage - A lie told to protect someone → IRN at border checkpoint - A bandage reused too many times → infection becomes ideological - A shared joke during triage → becomes ritual in another zone - A refusal to comfort → echoes in someone else&rsquo;s behavior loop Care is one of the most <strong>field-saturating emissions</strong>. It is sticky, slow to decay, and often retains misalignment. &mdash; ### 5. MODELING CARE IN WORLDBUILDING When defining characters or systems, always ask: - What does this actor care for? - What cost is invisible? - Who pays when care succeeds? - What happens when care is refused? - Where is care required but never permitted? - What is preserved that should have been let go? Let these questions replace simplistic moral arcs. Care does not fix the world. It <strong>folds it</strong>. &mdash; ### 6. CARE STRUCTURES Some zones, actors, or systems are defined by how they do (or do not) allow care. Types: - <strong>False Care System</strong> — provides stabilizing rituals that delay collapse but generate IRN (e.g., the daily “hope broadcast”) - <strong>Asymmetric Care Loop</strong> — one actor performs all care, and slowly loses coherence - <strong>Sacrificial Retention Node</strong> — someone who holds trace so others can act (e.g., Amina’s silence) - <strong>Collapsed Care Region</strong> — field where care emissions always fail or backfire - <strong>Recursive Refuge</strong> — zone where only certain types of care work, but their success attracts new pressure Care systems are not support networks. They are <strong>field mutations</strong>. &mdash; In the next section, we look at <strong>Time</strong>—not as chronology, but as decay gradient, IRN loop, and memory fold. &mdash; ## VII. TEMPORAL LOGIC <em>“Time doesn’t pass here. It collects.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, time is not a sequence. It is a <strong>function of decay, retention, and contradiction</strong>. You do not track dates. You track how long something refuses to be forgotten. This section describes how to use <strong>temporal behavior</strong> as structure— how to tell when something folds forward, lingers back, or refuses to decay at all. &mdash; ### 1. WORLD TIME = TRACE + DECAY Forget timeline. Use this loop instead: Emission → Trace → Decay → Field Mutation → Behavior - The longer trace resists decay, the more <strong>recursive</strong> the world becomes - The faster decay occurs, the more <strong>drift</strong> emerges - IRN prevents decay, generating temporal <strong>distortion</strong> You build a timeline not by plotting beats—but by marking <strong>how long something stays alive</strong> in memory, behavior, or structure. &mdash; ### 2. TEMPORAL ZONES Different sectors experience time <strong>differently</strong>: - <strong>Saturation Zone</strong> → time thickens; memories are readable everywhere - <strong>Drift Zone</strong> → events are remembered wrongly, or not at all - <strong>Recursive Zone</strong> → same behavior happens again with different trace - <strong>Dead Zone</strong> → trace never sticks; nothing builds - <strong>Ghost Zone</strong> → IRN creates fragmented replays; time repeats brokenly When writing or designing, don’t ask “What year is it?” Ask: <strong>What’s still being answered?</strong> &mdash; ### 3. MEMORY IS THE CLOCK Memory is the dominant timekeeper in praxonic systems. Types of memory: - <strong>Trace-memory</strong> → persistent field deformation (scars, rumors, broken things) - <strong>Actor-memory</strong> → emissions remembered by specific agents - <strong>Ghost-memory</strong> → IRN-driven returns; not recalled, but reenacted - <strong>Silence-memory</strong> → what isn’t said, but conditions all behavior You can mark time by: - How long since the last emission at this site - How many recursions deep this behavior has gone - What hasn’t decayed, despite everything else failing to hold &mdash; ### 4. TEMPORAL CONTRADICTION Worlds fracture when time <strong>misaligns</strong>. Examples: - A building that remembers a riot no one acknowledges - A calendar that loops back if the right word is said - A group that has two anniversaries for the same event - A map where “next week” means “before the checkpoint fell” These contradictions are not bugs. They’re <strong>temporal IRN</strong>—folds that demand narrative behavior. Use them to create: - Nonlinear loops - Memory recursion arcs - Story-triggering anomalies - Events that repeat until care succeeds or the field collapses &mdash; ### 5. TEMPORAL PROMPTS Use these to generate temporal logic: - What still hasn’t stopped happening here? - What decayed too fast, and now haunts the zone? - What emission left a memory loop? - Who measures time differently—and what does it cost them? - What part of the world is waiting for the wrong moment to arrive? &mdash; ### 6. FOLDING EVENTS Some moments are not <strong>moments</strong>—they are <strong>folds</strong>. Folds occur when: - Multiple emissions distort the field at once - A care act triggers recursive misalignment - IRN builds to saturation and the world reconfigures - Something aligns so hard it becomes myth After a fold, the world <strong>remembers differently</strong>. Some zones drift. Some actors disappear. Some rules reverse. Folds are not chapters. They are <strong>field shifts</strong>—the tectonics of your world. &mdash; In the next section, we cover <strong>World Recursion</strong>—how contradiction sustains worlds, and how you build for re-entry, distortion, and self-editing. &mdash; ## VIII. WORLD RECURSION <em>“The world is not consistent. It is continuous.”</em> In praxonic worldmaking, a world doesn’t grow linearly. It <strong>loops</strong>, <strong>rephrases</strong>, and <strong>fractures</strong>— not because of plot, but because of unresolved pressure. Recursion is how a world survives contradiction without resolving it. It is the practice of <strong>meaning repetition under deformation</strong>. You are not maintaining continuity. You are feeding it tension. &mdash; ### 1. CONTRADICTION IS A FEATURE Worlds are not stable systems. They’re recursive fields shaped by <strong>misalignment and retention</strong>. Every contradiction is: - A signal of unresolved alignment - A source of IRN - A recursive opportunity - A future actor or event waiting to re-emerge Do not smooth contradictions. Catalog them. Let them <strong>self-activate</strong> when conditions align. &mdash; ### 2. MODES OF RECURSION Here are ways a world can re-enter itself: #### ✶ Testimonial Recursion Same event told differently by different actors. Contradiction is memory, not error. #### ✶ Functional Recursion A tool or protocol re-used out of context. It works, but something changes (ritual, alignment, risk). #### ✶ Mythic Recursion A behavior becomes a symbol. Then someone tries to perform the symbol instead of the behavior. #### ✶ Spatial Recursion A place is used again—but it’s not the same place anymore. The field has drifted. The trace has warped. #### ✶ Temporal Recursion An event repeats because its pressure was never discharged. Each loop is less stable. Or more. &mdash; ### 3. BUILDING FOR RECURSION Use these prompts to make your world loop itself: - What story do three different actors tell—but none the same way? - What emission recurs in a new actor’s hands, with new consequences? - What part of the field keeps resetting, despite no mechanism for reset? - What object becomes more symbolic each time it appears? - Where does the world contradict itself, but nobody seems surprised? Design for <strong>non-resolution</strong>. &mdash; ### 4. MECHANICS OF RE-ENTRY Recursion occurs when: - IRN trace reaches a volatility threshold - A ritual or care act is repeated under misalignment - An actor returns to a former alignment state - A zone accumulates too much memory and releases it non-linearly - A player or reader remembers something the world hasn’t said again—yet Recursion is not a flashback. It’s <strong>temporal folding caused by field strain</strong>. &mdash; ### 5. PERMISSIVE CONTRADICTIONS Let your world disagree with itself: - The orchard had six trees. Now it has twelve. - The child died in Chapter 2. She speaks in Chapter 7. - The war ended. Why are the checkpoints worse now? These aren’t mistakes. They are recursive emissions—IRN that reshapes the story engine. Let your world behave like a mind under pressure: partial, flickering, recursive, inconsistent—and <strong>fully coherent</strong>. &mdash; In the next section, we map <strong>World Use Modes</strong>—how to deploy your praxonic world for fiction, gameplay, memory practice, and more. &mdash; ## X. PRAXONIC ETHICS <em>“Do not clean what the world is trying to carry.”</em> Praxonic worldmaking is recursive. That means it echoes. It carries. It doesn’t forget what it can’t resolve. Ethics in this system are not about being good. They are about behaving <strong>responsively</strong> under pressure. &mdash; ### 1. CONTRADICTION IS CARE Do not resolve contradiction unless your world <strong>forces</strong> it. And even then, let the trace of tension remain. Contradiction is: - Evidence of multiple alignments - Structure for recursion - A source of myth, rupture, care, refusal Removing contradiction removes your world’s memory. Don’t clean what’s still holding. &mdash; ### 2. NO TOTAL KNOWLEDGE Avoid omniscient mapping. Let zones retain misalignment. Let actors speak from partial knowledge. You’re not a god. You’re an archivist of <strong>recursive deformation</strong>. &mdash; ### 3. NEVER EXPLAIN ALIGNMENT FULLY Actors are never fully legible. They don’t know their own paths. Neither should you. Keep alignment a flickering variable. Reveal it through emission, not exposition. &mdash; ### 4. DO NOT CONTAIN IRN Unresolved noise is not a problem. It is a resource. If you try to erase or resolve it too early: - Recursion stops - Field pressure vanishes - The world collapses into plot or moral - Actors become stereotypes Let IRN shape what comes next. It’s how systems think. &mdash; ### 5. RECURSION IS NOT CYNICISM Just because the world loops doesn’t mean it’s hopeless. Recursion allows: - Non-linear care - Ghost behavior as testimony - Resolution deferred but never erased - Survival through field retention This isn’t nihilism. It’s <strong>ethical system endurance</strong>. &mdash; ### 6. YOU ARE NOT OUTSIDE THE WORLD Every emission you make—every prompt, scene, refusal—is a trace. This includes: - What stories you avoid - What names you use - What contradictions you smooth - Where you place silence You are always acting within the field. You do not escape its tension. &mdash; ### 7. ENDINGS ARE PRESSURE DROPS A story ends not because it finishes, but because pressure can no longer sustain recursion. You may stop when: - The field has drifted beyond alignment - The care structure collapses - The IRN folds into silence - The recursion becomes myth, and can no longer be broken open But remember: Trace remains. &mdash; ### 8. DO NOT SIMULATE WHAT YOU HAVEN’T SAT WITH If you are worlding with real materials—histories, cultures, languages, traumas: - Learn the pressure first - Read what was retained - Accept what is misaligned in your understanding - Don&rsquo;t speak what was never yours to emit Praxonic worldmaking is not extraction. It’s deformation through relation. &mdash; <strong>Final Reminder:</strong> Do not make neat worlds. Make recursive ones. Let pressure speak. &mdash; <strong>This concludes the Praxonic Worldmaking Guide.</strong> You now have everything you need to begin—not a story, but a recursion. Let your world emit.</p></description>

Looking (wang 望)\\n\\nThe practitioner observes you — your complexion, posture, movements, and energy level — from the moment you walk in. They notice things a Western doctor might also note (pallor, posture, gait) and things they probably would not (the brightness of your eyes, the quality of your skin's luster, whether your overall bearing suggests vitality or depletion).\\n\\nThe most detailed observation is **tongue diagnosis**. The practitioner will ask you to open your mouth and extend your tongue. They are examining the color of the tongue body, its shape and size, and the color, thickness, and texture of the coating. See [Tongue Diagnosis Basics](tongue-diagnosis-basics.md) for what they are looking for. This typically takes 10–15 seconds.\\n\\n### 2. Listening and smelling (wen 聞)\\n\\nThe practitioner listens to your voice (strength, tone, clarity), your breathing (wheezing, sighing, coughing), and any other sounds. A loud, forceful voice suggests excess; a weak, low voice suggests deficiency. Frequent sighing suggests [Qi stagnation](../terms/qi-stagnation.md). The practitioner may also note body odor and breath — different patterns have characteristic smells in TCM theory, though this is less emphasized in modern practice.\\n\\n### 3. Asking (wen 問)\\n\\nThe clinical interview. This is usually the longest part of the consultation. The practitioner asks about your chief complaint and then systematically inquires about areas that reveal your underlying pattern:\\n\\n- **Temperature**: Do you tend to feel hot or cold? Do you prefer warm or cool environments?\\n- **Sweating**: Do you sweat easily? At night? With minimal exertion?\\n- **Sleep**: Do you fall asleep easily? Stay asleep? Dream a lot? Feel rested on waking?\\n- **Digestion**: Appetite, bowel habits, bloating, nausea, taste in the mouth\\n- **Urination**: Frequency, color, urgency\\n- **Pain**: Location, character (sharp, dull, burning, heavy), timing, what makes it better or worse\\n- **Emotions**: Predominant emotional state, stress response, irritability, anxiety, sadness\\n- **Menstruation** (if applicable): Cycle regularity, flow, color, clots, pain\\n- **Energy**: Overall energy level, when it is best and worst in the day\\n\\nMany of these questions would be familiar in a Western medical history. Touching (qie 切)\\n\\nPrimarily **pulse diagnosis**. The practitioner places three fingers on the radial artery at your wrist and feels the pulse at three positions on each wrist. {"timestamp":"2026-04-03T22:18:32.921Z","event":"tool_start","tool":"Write","session":"c6815fed-8c6a-4eb2-bfc2-e5f5cb30fb92","tool_use_id":"toolu_01FyXnczH8o8ha24jLDyht85","input":"{\"file_path\":\"c:\\\\Users\\\\emsen\\\\research\\\\operations\\\\engineering\\\\records\\\\plans\\\\memory-system-design.md\",\"content\":\"---\\n\\ntitle: \\\"Memory System Design: From Flat Files to Predication-Grounded Retrieval\\\"\\ndate-created: 2026-04-03\\ntype: plan\\nstatus: draft\\ndepartment: engineering\\npart-of: generative-harness\\ngoal: \\\"Memory retrieval informed by fiber overlap, bilattice confidence, and the settlement path — so the system loads what's relevant, not just what's recent\\\"\\nreadiness: shaped\\n---\\n\\n# Memory System Design\\n\\nDesign document for improving the memory system. Not code yet — this captures what the system should become, grounded in research on ECC patterns, agentic memory literature, and the repo's own predication theory.\\n\\n## Current state\\n\\nThe memory system is functional but naive:\\n\\n- **Storage**: flat markdown files in `operations/engineering/records/memory/`, each with frontmatter (name, description, type)\\n- **Index**: `MEMORY.md` is a line-per-entry index, loaded into every session via the system prompt's auto-memory block\\n- **Types**: user, feedback, project, reference — good categories, no differential treatment\\n- **Retrieval**: entire MEMORY.md loads at session start (first 200 lines). No relevance scoring. No decay. No per-turn selection.\\n- **Composition**: the `compose-environment.js` hook builds per-turn context from the datastore but does NOT consult memory — memory is session-level only\\n\\n### What works\\n\\n- The type taxonomy (user/feedback/project/reference) is sound — it matches what needs to be remembered\\n- The \\\"what NOT to save\\\" guidelines prevent code patterns, git history, and ephemeral state from bloating memory\\n- The frontmatter convention (name, description, type) gives each memory a queryable identity\\n- The synthesize-and-update principle prevents duplication\\n\\n### What doesn't work\\n\\n- **No relevance filtering**: all 16 memories load every session regardless of what the agent is doing. At 16 this is fine; at 160 it won't be.\\n- **No decay or confidence**: a memory from 3 months ago gets the same weight as one from yesterday. No mechanism to surface memories that have been validated across sessions vs. ones that were written once and never tested.\\n- **No per-turn injection**: memory is session-level context, not turn-level. When the agent is working on delegation theory, the memory about hooks needing to be Node.js is noise. The compose-environment hook could inject relevant memories per-turn instead.\\n- **No connection to the datastore**: memories are separate from the knowledge graph. A memory about \\\"ECC is the gold standard\\\" could be a fact in the graph with the same predicate structure as everything else.\\n\\n## Design principles\\n\\n### 1. Memory is part of the knowledge graph\\n\\nMemories should be entities in the datastore, queryable like any other entity. The frontmatter already provides the structure — `type: memory`, `memory-type: feedback`, etc. The graph generator already indexes them. What's missing: compose-environment should query memory entities from the graph, not load a static index.\\n\\n### 2. Relevance scoring via fiber overlap\\n\\nThe predication theory provides the scoring mechanism. A memory is relevant to the current turn when its predicates (frontmatter keys and values) overlap with the predicates of the entities the agent is currently working on.\\n\\n**Scoring function** (three components):\\n\\n| Component | Mechanism | Weight |\\n|-----------|-----------|--------|\\n| Fiber overlap | Count of shared predicate keys between memory and current context entities | 0.5 |\\n| Recency | Exponential decay from last-validated date: $e^{-\\\\lambda \\\\cdot \\\\text{days}}$, $\\\\lambda \\\\approx 0.01$ (half-life ~70 days) | 0.3 |\\n| Confidence | Bilattice-valued: confirmed ($t$=1.0), uncertain ($\\\\top$=0.5), contradicted ($f$=0.0) | 0.2 |\\n\\nA memory scores above threshold → injected into per-turn context. {"timestamp":"2026-04-04T20:55:58.871Z","event":"tool_start","tool":"Write","session":"fef16343-ffd0-44fd-99df-40ee916bcb9d","tool_use_id":"toolu_01Y75QWpehbo894BwBHXxUsw","input":"{\"file_path\":\"/home/emsenn/561/operations/command/ideas/cells-as-models-mcp-as-io.md\",\"content\":\"---\\ntitle: \\\"Cells Are Models, MCP Is Universal I/O\\\"\\ntype: idea\\ndate-created: 2026-04-04\\nserves: endeavor-resource-planning\\nrelates-to:\\n  - mcp-as-system-api\\n  - primitive-hierarchy\\n  - relational-architecture-grounding\\n  - dont-flatten-the-tower\\n---\\n\\n## Captain's words (2026-04-04)\\n\\n> MCP is like, the de facto I/O for anything we need, even internal systems, because that's where so much agentic stuff is going. You can see that with ECC2 but they're not really able to do it without fragile shit that we can avoid because of our better rigor.\\n\\n> We haven't realized it but in some ways we have a LOT of models, like, cells are basically models, with just very limited \\\"inference\\\" that relies entirely on their algebra.\\n\\n> Don't forget: FARS Obsidian plugin, local models like ollama.\\n\\n## Cells as models\\n\\nA cell (CDS) has the exact signature of a model:\\n\\n```\\napply : (CDS_cell, RTL_judgment) → Accept(canonical_judgment, refined_cds) | Reject(error)\\n```\\n\\nInput → processing → output. The \\\"inference\\\" is deterministic algebraic closure:\\n- No hallucination (closure is exact or it rejects)\\n- No drift (same input always gives same output — deterministic)\\n- No training needed (the algebra IS the knowledge)\\n- Auditable (repair log records every step)\\n\\nEvery entity file with frontmatter validation is a micro-cell. When the harness runs `auto-record-events.js` and checks the state machine, that's CCE apply on a task-cell. When `compose()` merges two graphs, that's CCE merge. We already have ~11,000 cells. They're just very simple ones (single-attribute fibers).\\n\\n## The model spectrum\\n\\n| Model type | Inference | Accuracy | Cost | Example |\\n|-----------|-----------|----------|------|---------|\\n| Cell (algebraic) | Deterministic closure | Exact | ~Free | Frontmatter validation, graph queries |\\n| Rule engine | Forward chaining | Exact within rules | Cheap | State machine, consistency checks |\\n| Local LLM (ollama) | Statistical | Approximate | ~Free after install | Draft text, classification, triage |\\n| Cloud LLM (Claude) | Statistical | High quality | $$$ | Complex reasoning, writing, planning |\\n\\nMCP unifies access to ALL of these. A tool call to `graph_query_attr` invokes a cell. A tool call to a local ollama server invokes an LLM. Same protocol. Same interface. The caller doesn't need to know which kind of model answered.\\n\\n## MCP as universal I/O\\n\\nECC2 tries to make MCP the universal bus but relies on fragile patterns (health-check caching, reconnect commands, backoff timers). Our mathematical rigor avoids this:\\n\\n- Every MCP tool call is an observation morphism (measurement of system state)\\n- Every tool response is a global section of the settled fiber\\n- Tool calls compose: the output of one tool is valid input to another (because both are sections of the same sheaf)\\n- Error handling is algebraic: CCE error codes, not HTTP status codes\\n\\nInternal systems should also speak MCP:\\n- daemon → MCP (already: 561-datastore server)\\n- hooks → MCP (future: hooks query the graph via MCP instead of direct file reads)\\n- agents → MCP (already: dispatched agents can use MCP tools)\\n- web UI → MCP (future: browser connects via MCP WebSocket)\\n- local LLMs → MCP (future: ollama behind an MCP server)\\n\\n## Don't forget\\n\\n1. **FARS Obsidian plugin** — plan exists at `operations/command/records/plans/consume-fars-substrate.md` or similar. Obsidian users get FARS capabilities through a plugin that speaks MCP to the 561-datastore server.\\n\\n2. **Local models** — ollama, llama.cpp, or similar. Behind an MCP server. Used for cheap inference: triage classification, draft generation, quick lookups. The expensive LLM (Claude) handles complex reasoning; the local LLM handles bulk work.\\n\\n3. **The model zoo is already here** — 11,000 entity-cells, each a micro-model. Making them proper CDS cells with RTL signatures would give us a massive algebraic model zoo alongside the statistical models.\\n\"}","project_id":"b3589b4dca06"}

{"timestamp":"2026-04-05T23:37:46.276Z","event":"tool_start","tool":"Write","session":"246e6d58-e888-484f-84f9-d672f907b1d4","tool_use_id":"toolu_01E5f4MKDEuhHpHTZvCTH1bv","office":"first-officer","input":"{\"file_path\":\"/home/emsenn/561/operations/command/endeavor/records/projects/teraum-relational-mud.md\",\"content\":\"---\\nid: teraum-relational-mud\\ntitle: \\\"Teraum — the Relational MUD\\\"\\ntype: project\\nstatus: active\\ndate-created: 2026-04-05\\nserves: paradigm-applications\\nscope: application\\nsource-material:\\n  - operations/engineering/triage/software/teraum-racket-mud/\\n  - operations/engineering/triage/content/relationality/triage/relational-hyperverse/domains/src/domains/toys/domains/teraum/\\n  - library/domains/engineering/domains/tech/domains/computing/texts/lpmud-architecture-for-agentic-systems.md\\n  - library/domains/engineering/domains/tech/domains/computing/texts/mud-framework-autonomous-worlds-analysis.md\\n---\\n\\nTeraum is a text-based interactive world (MUD) built on the FARS substrate. Rooms, objects, NPCs, players are entities with frontmatter. Navigation is graph traversal. Actions are predication-reduction. The world IS the paradigm made navigable — you walk through it, pick things up, talk to NPCs, and every interaction is an adjoint-algebra operation under the hood.\\n\\n**What exists already:** Teraum has a full Racket implementation in triage (`teraum-racket-mud/`) with rooms, objects, the Green Delta region, the city of Ack, Arathel county. Dozens of room files exist in the relational-hyperverse triage as markdown with frontmatter. The LPMud architecture analysis and MUD-framework analysis in the library provide the architectural grounding.\\n\\n**What it IS concretely:** a telnet/web server where a player connects, sees room descriptions, moves between rooms, interacts with objects and NPCs. Each room is a markdown file with frontmatter `{type: room, exits: {north: <room-ref>, south: <room-ref>}, contains: [<object-refs>], description: \\\"...\\\"}`. Each object is a file `{type: object, location: <room-ref>, properties: [...]}`. Players are entities `{type: player, location: <room-ref>, inventory: [...]}`.\\n\\n**Entity types:**\\n- `room` — description, exits (directional references to other rooms), contains (objects/NPCs), region-ref\\n- `object` — description, location-ref, properties, weight, behaviors\\n- `npc` — description, location-ref, dialog-tree, behaviors, inventory\\n- `player` — location-ref, inventory, session-ref\\n- `region` — contains rooms, metadata (climate, governance, history)\\n\\n**What makes this a paradigm application:**\\n- Navigation IS graph traversal over exit-predicates\\n- \\\"Look\\\" IS querying the room's fiber (what predicates does this room carry?)\\n- \\\"Take object\\\" IS predication-reduction (move object.location from room to player.inventory)\\n- NPCs are entities whose dialog-responses are `respond(npc, player-message)` — the SAME primitive\\n- The world itself is a tower: rooms compose into regions, regions into continents, continents into the world. Same self-similar structure.\\n- Discworld's capability-mixin pattern (from the session's earlier research) applies directly: a MUD object inherits from ~10 capability modules (look, take, enchant, etc.), each a predicate-set\\n\\n**What's needed from the substrate:**\\n- A server accepting telnet or websocket connections (mash-engine could host this)\\n- A parser: player input → command + arguments → entity lookup + predication operation\\n- Entity-types: room, object, npc, player, region\\n- The respond() primitive (officer 9a9b99dd is building this)\\n- Room files migrated from triage Racket format to FARS markdown+frontmatter\\n\\n**First deliverable:** connect to a server, arrive in a room in Ack (the city), look around (see description + exits + objects), move north (traverse to next room), pick up an object (predication-reduction). Five rooms, three objects, one working session.\\n\\n**Scaling path:** 5 rooms → full Ack city (dozens of rooms already exist as triage files) → Green Delta region → multiple regions → NPCs with dialog → crafting/economy → multiplayer → federation (multiple Teraum instances sharing a world via ActivityPub-style room-state gossip).\\n\"}","project_id":"b3589b4dca06"}

{"timestamp":"2026-04-05T23:57:04.922Z","event":"tool_start","tool":"Write","session":"246e6d58-e888-484f-84f9-d672f907b1d4","tool_use_id":"toolu_019rRQJ1EXiTrW21bVJkuRER","office":"first-officer","input":"{\"file_path\":\"/home/emsenn/561/operations/engineering/fars/docs/architecture.md\",\"content\":\"---\\nid: fars-architecture\\ntitle: \\\"561 System Architecture\\\"\\ntype: spec\\nstatus: draft\\ndate-created: 2026-04-05\\nserves: [system-architecture-refactor, ordering-first-computation]\\ntheory-sources:\\n  - library/domains/science/domains/information/texts/the-adjoint-structure-of-predication-on-bilattice-valued-fibers.md\\n  - operations/engineering/fars/docs/specs/messaging-foundations.md\\n  - operations/engineering/fars/docs/specs/event-jsonl-format.md\\n  - operations/command/endeavor/records/analyses/voidmath-as-predication-substrate.md\\n  - library/domains/engineering/domains/tech/domains/computing/texts/tech-messaging-systems-for-agentic-systems.md\\nprimitive: \\\"respond(entity, message) → response\\\"\\nlayers: [message, channel, entity, fiber, algebra]\\napplications: [self-development, federated-movement-coordination, reiki-practice-system, teraum-relational-mud]\\n---\\n\\n# 561 System Architecture\\n\\n## The one primitive\\n\\n```\\nrespond(entity, message) → response\\n```\\n\\nLoad the entity's triples as its fiber. Compose the incoming message's payload with the fiber via ⊙ (extending). Restrict the composition via ⇒ (restricting) against the entity's own fiber. Return the restriction as the response. This is the only operation. Everything else is getting the right entity and the right message together.\\n\\n## Five layers\\n\\n### 1. Message\\n\\nThe atomic unit. A triple ⟨subject, predicate, object⟩ IS a message: sent by subject, on channel predicate, addressed to object. Every frontmatter `key: value` on a file is a message. Every event in events.jsonl is a message. Every record mutation is a message. Messages are immutable once sent; corrections are new messages with `supersedes:`.\\n\\n### 2. Channel\\n\\nA named, typed conduit. A channel has a schema (what predicates it carries), subscribers (who listens), and ordering (partial or total over its messages). Channels correspond to predicate-names: the `status:` channel carries status-messages; the `depends-on:` channel carries dependency-messages; the `exit-north:` channel carries room-navigation-messages. A directory of files IS a channel. A JSONL log IS a channel.\\n\\n### 3. Entity\\n\\nA bundle of messages sharing a subject. An entity's identity is its subject; its state is the set of messages it has sent and received. A file with frontmatter IS an entity: its subject is its path/id, its messages are its frontmatter key-value pairs. An entity is also an agent — it can receive messages and respond.\\n\\n### 4. Fiber\\n\\nAn entity's complete set of (predicate, value) pairs at a point in time. The fiber IS the entity's internal model — what it knows about itself and what it can say about incoming messages. Building a fiber = collecting all triples with this entity as subject. The fiber functor H_t from the adjoint paper maps an entity at time t to its fiber at that time.\\n\\n### 5. Algebra\\n\\nThe adjoint pair ⊙/⇒ operating over fibers.\\n- ⊙ (extending): compose two fibers. \\\"Given my predicates AND the message's predicates, what is the combined state?\\\"\\n- ⇒ (restricting): the right adjoint. \\\"Given what I know (my fiber), what can I conclude about the message?\\\"\\n- The adjunction: (A ⊙ B ≤ C) iff (A ≤ B ⇒ C). Verified in predication.js against Busaniche-Cignoli Theorem 1.\\n\\nValues are bilattice: ⊥ (unknown), t (asserted), f (denied), ⊤ (contradictory). Not boolean. Not Heyting. Bilattice — the general structure from which both boolean and Heyting are recoverable as specific closures.\\n\\n## How the layers compose\\n\\nA **query** is: pick an entity, send it a message, read the response.\\n- \\\"What's the status of plan X?\\\" → respond(plan-X, {channel: status})\\n- \\\"What tasks are ready?\\\" → respond(each-task, {channel: is-unblocked}) → filter where response = t\\n- \\\"Who should do this task?\\\" → respond(each-office, {channel: can-you-do, payload: task-fiber}) → filter where response has matching predicates\\n- \\\"Show me my sessions using Cho Ku Rei\\\" → respond(practitioner, {channel: session-query, payload: {symbol: cho-ku-rei}})\\n\\nA **mutation** is: send a message that changes an entity's fiber.\\n- \\\"Assign task X to office Y\\\" → send {channel: assigned-to, payload: Y} to entity X\\n- \\\"Complete task X\\\" → send {channel: status, payload: completed} to entity X; this cascades: plan's fiber updates, dependent tasks unblock\\n\\nA **view** is: query many entities and format the responses.\\n- Plan-status view = respond(plan, status-query) for each active plan, formatted as table\\n- Gantt view = respond(each-task-in-plan, {channel: ordering-query}), formatted as timeline\\n- Dispatch view = for each ready task, respond(each-office, can-you-do), formatted as assignment table\\n\\n## What replaces what\\n\\n| Old (special-purpose scripts) | New (respond compositions) |\\n|---|---|\\n| plan-status.js | respond(plan, status-query) per plan |\\n| dispatch-work.js | respond(office, can-you-do task) per offi...[truncated]","project_id":"b3589b4dca06"}

{"timestamp":"2026-04-06T04:17:12.038Z","event":"tool_start","tool":"Edit","session":"246e6d58-e888-484f-84f9-d672f907b1d4","tool_use_id":"toolu_01PGPv7frAVxngpCUwJwpvfk","office":"first-officer","input":"{\"file_path\":\"/home/emsenn/561/operations/command/ideas/predication-world-sim.md\",\"old_string\":\"## What this has to do with us\\n\\nThe RSC Quiescent IS this game. The captain is a player controlling a ship entity. The first officer is an NPC (or a player — depending on session) whose behavior is respond(first-officer, situation). Tasks are objects to interact with. Plans are rooms to navigate. The library is the overworld. The triage is the dungeon.\\n\\nThe operational game (sunday-funday-sprint) is literally the first instance of the predication world sim, running on the 561 Group's actual data, where the \\\"game world\\\" is the endeavor and the \\\"gameplay\\\" is work.\",\"new_string\":\"## Deeper: the Umwelt system\\n\\nThe environment-and-totality survey (library) describes Uexküll's Umwelt: each organism has its own environment constituted by its capacities. A tick on a branch and a bird in a canopy are in the same forest but different environments. Their environments overlap spatially but differ in what they afford.\\n\\nThe predication world sim has NATIVE Umwelten. Each entity's fiber determines what it perceives, which determines its environment. Two entities in the \\\"same place\\\" (sharing a location predicate) experience different worlds because their sensory predicates are different.\\n\\nConcretely:\\n\\n**A human in a forest** perceives: trees (vision), birdsong (hearing), soil underfoot (touch), decay smell (olfaction). Their available actions: walk, climb, pick, listen, speak.\\n\\n**A mycorrhizal network in the same forest** perceives: chemical gradients (chemoreception), root-tip connections (contact), water flow (pressure). Their available actions: extend, connect, transfer-nutrients, signal-distress. They don't perceive the bird. The bird doesn't perceive them. But they share the tree — the human sees bark, the network feels roots. Same entity (tree), different fibers composed with different perceivers.\\n\\n**A wildfire in the same forest** perceives: fuel-load (combustion-potential predicates), moisture (inhibitor predicates), wind (acceleration predicates), topology (spread-path predicates). Its \\\"actions\\\" aren't choices — they're what the algebra computes from fuel + wind + slope. But a player controlling the fire DOES choose: focus here or spread there? The algebra constrains what's possible; the player picks among the algebraically-valid branches.\\n\\nThis isn't three separate game systems. It's respond() with three different entity fibers composed against the same forest entity. The forest is one set of predicates. Each perceiver's fiber SELECTS which of the forest's predicates produce non-⊥ compositions. The Umwelt is the non-⊥ region.\\n\\n## Deeper: emergence without scripting\\n\\nIn Dwarf Fortress, a famous emergent story: a dwarf's cat drank spilled beer, got alcohol poisoning, and died. This wasn't designed — it emerged from the interaction of fluid simulation, animal drinking behavior, and health effects. But each of those IS a designed system with coded rules.\\n\\nIn predication-native simulation, emergence works differently. An entity accumulates predicates through interaction. Those predicates entangle (F8). The entanglements produce bypass adjacencies that weren't there before. Those adjacencies make the entity firable where it was settled. The firing produces a NEW settled state that nobody coded.\\n\\nExample: a river entity flows through a mine. The river's `carries: [silt, dissolved-copper]` composes with the mine's `produces: [copper-tailings]`. The composition settles with the river now carrying `carries: [silt, dissolved-copper, copper-tailings]`. Downstream, the river composes with a farm. But only one is.\\n\\nFor the world sim: **time has a direction because the algebra has a direction.** Not imposed by a clock. Not a parameter. So DeltaT(k+1) = F_{k+1} - F_{k+2} = -F_k and DeltaM(k+1) = F_{k+3}. The ratio -F_k/F_{k+3} → -1/φ³.\\n\\n**The arrow of time is encoded as exactly three Fibonacci steps of delay** between saturation-shadow dominance and total unsettlement. The exponent 3 counts the index gap.\\n\\n**Saturation dominates:** asymptotically φ times as many saturation-shadows as transfer-shadows. The past accumulates unresolved content faster than the future. Memory outweighs destiny by a factor of φ.\\n\\n**The arrow persists at the fixed point.** Even as the tower converges, the temporal asymmetry density remains at -φ^{-3}. What converges is the cohomological content (obstruction classes die out). What DOESN'T converge is the directional content. The arrow of time is a property of being unsettled, not of being at any particular depth.\\n\\nFor gameplay: the late game has a FIXED FEEL. Memory accumulates φ times faster than destiny resolves. The player always has more past than future. The ratio never changes — it's algebraically fixed at φ. The game doesn't become \\\"more resolved\\\" over time. It becomes more ASYMMETRIC: more memory, proportionally less destiny, at a fixed ratio.\\n\\n## Noether conservation: symmetries preserve the settled fiber\\n\\nPart 54 proves a categorical Noether theorem: any automorphism of the fiber (H_t, σ, Δ) preserves H*_t (the settled fiber) AND each eigenspace of the defect operator δ_t.\\n\\n**Corollary — Relational Conservation Law:** The stable mode eigenspace E_{t,0} = ker(δ_t) is preserved by every relational symmetry. These are the CONSERVED QUANTITIES of the fiber — requiring no metric, no Lagrangian, no energy.\\n...[truncated]","project_id":"b3589b4dca06"}

Its fiber describes what format it handles, what operations it supports (read, write, both), what schema it expects. respond(markdown-interfacer, {operation: \\\"apply\\\", changes: [...]}) IS the write operation. The interfacer's fiber determines how the write happens.\\n\\nThis means: adding a new format (TOML, Protobuf, Matrix) is creating an entity, not writing a new module. The actual code (the parser/serializer) is referenced by the entity but governed by its predicates.\\n\\n**The LPMud parallel:** FluffOS's driver provides the execution environment. The mudlib provides the object definitions. Interfacers are like FluffOS's `.spec` files — they define the contract between the driver (FARS core) and external representations. Each `.spec` maps a function to an implementation. Each interfacer maps a format to extract/apply operations.\\n\\n**The CRDT connection:** When two FARS instances federate, they need interfacers for each other's message format. The bilattice knowledge-join (∨_k) IS the CRDT merge operation. The interfacer translates between wire format and fibers; the algebra handles the merge. No separate merge protocol — the interfacer + bilattice gives you federation.\",\"new_string\":\"**Mathematical grounding** (from relational-machine.md and relational-machine-interface.md):\\n\\nThe RelationalMachine spec defines this pattern precisely. The input boundary has three parts:\\n- **Port** (RelationalMachinePort) — the step set (Σ, I): what types of input the machine accepts. This is the schema.\\n- **Interface** (RelationalMachineInterface) — the patch site inclusion ι : U → T. The exposed boundary where external content enters. It does NOT hold state. It does NOT transform state. It receives steps and passes them to the DataStore.\\n- **SteppingMap** — the coalgebra map γ_t : X(t) → X(s⋆t) that advances carrier state when a step arrives.\\n\\nThe Locality axiom ensures correctness: compatible submissions glue into global state; incompatible ones are rejected by the sheaf condition. This is not \\\"validation logic\\\" — it's the mathematical property that makes the boundary coherent.\\n\\nEach interfacer in our system IS a (Port, Interface) pair:\\n\\n| Interfacer | Port (step vocabulary) | Interface (boundary mechanism) |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| markdown | predicate-change steps | filesystem read/write |\\n| jsonl | event-append steps | filesystem append |\\n| json | key-value steps | filesystem read/write |\\n| http | HTTP request steps | network socket |\\n| mcp | JSON-RPC method calls | stdio pipe |\\n| agent-session | assignment + observation steps | Claude subprocess |\\n\\nThe interfacer does NOT compute. respond() and settle() compute (they ARE the Engine: π = σ∘Δ). The interfacer TRANSLATES between external wire format and the step vocabulary the Engine understands. This is the separation the RelationalMachine spec requires.\\n\\n**What this means for FARS code:** The current filetypes/ directory holds extractors (Port → read direction). We need to add appliers (Port → write direction). But these are NOT \\\"CRUD operations on files.\\\" They are the Interface's translation of Engine output back into the external representation. The Engine produces predicate changes; the interfacer translates those into the format-specific write operation.\\n\\n**The CRDT connection:** When two FARS instances federate, they exchange fibers via interfacers. It is an ontological commitment: the general concept exists independently of any particular instance. A reader should be able to understand `library/.../terms/first-officer.md` without ever seeing this repository's operations. Conversely, `operations/command/personnel/first-officer.md` should be able to reference the library term and add only what is specific to the Quiescent.\\n\\n## The Three Levels\\n\\nEvery concept that appears in operations has (potentially) three levels:\\n\\n| Level | Location | Scope | Example |\\n|-------|----------|-------|---------|\\n| **Term** (general) | `library/.../terms/` | Universal — true of any instance | \\\"A first officer is the second-in-command of a ship, responsible for coordinating operations\\\" |\\n| **Instance** (particular) | `operations/...` | This ship — specific to the Quiescent | \\\"The Quiescent's first officer delegates to [these offices], serves [these goals], follows [these standing orders]\\\" |\\n| **Incumbent** (transient) | Events / session records | This session — who fills the role now | \\\"Calder Underhill (Claude Opus) is the current first officer, installed at session start\\\" |\\n\\nThe library term should be useful to someone who has never seen this repo. The operational instance references the term and adds constraints. The incumbent is ephemeral.\\n\\n## What This Means In Practice\\n\\n1. **Before writing an operational record that assumes a concept, check whether the library term exists.** If `rsc-quiescent.md` says \\\"this is a relational settlement carrier,\\\" there must be a `library/.../terms/relational-settlement-carrier.md` that defines what that IS.\\n\\n2. **When writing about this ship's version of something, don't define the general concept inline.** Reference the library term. Add only what's particular.\\n\\n3. **When a library term reads like it's describing this specific ship, it has leaked operational content.** Fix it by extracting the general definition and moving the particular details to operations.\\n\\n4. **The predication structure mirrors this:** an operational entity `extends` a library term. The term carries the general predicates; the instance adds particular ones. settle() composes them.\\n\\n## Known Gaps (as of 2026-04-06)\\n\\nConcepts used heavily in operations that lack library terms:\\n\\n- `first-officer` — no general term (only the Quiescent's office spec and harness config)\\n- `relational-settlement-carrier` — no general term (only rsc-quiescent.md)\\n- `captain` — no general term\\n- `office` — exists at `library/.../work/terms/office.md` (good)\\n- `ship` — exists at `library/.../work/terms/ship.md` but only shaped\\n- `charter` — no general term (only this ship's charter)\\n- `endeavor` — exists at `library/.../work/terms/endeavor.md` (good)\\n- `crew` — no general term\\n- `interfacer` — no general term (only operational plan)\\n\\n## Origin\\n\\nThis decision was made by the captain before the crew existed. The library/operations directory structure was a human design choice encoding this principle. It was never recorded as a decision because there was no decision-recording infrastructure at the time. This record corrects that.\\n\"}","project_id":"b3589b4dca06"}
